If I'm being brutally, BRUTALLY honest, this isn't quite what I was hoping for in a successor to the Jet Set Radio games. Now I mean, don't get me wrong, after 20 something years, I'm glad we got SOMETHING but... see, it's like being forced to try vegan bacon when you've been raised on actual meaty bacon for so long. It's just not the same. No matter how hard you try to convince yourself of the minimal difference, it's still different enough that it simply can't quite hit that same level Jet Set Radio had.

For one, the game is kind of missing a lot of what gave Jet Set Radio it's personality. Like DJ Professor K, aka the guy who basically narrated a lot of the story in JSR while also hosting the pirate radio station that played the awesome soundtrack. Bomb Rush unfortunately lacks a character like that and while in JSR, all the music in the game was available from the beginning, you have to go out and actively FIND the music in collectibles in BRC. The method of story-telling is also done directly through the characters too, which while I don't mind, I feel like they could've done it a bit better than they did. In spite of the fact that characters interact with each other, I can't help but feel a disturbing lack of personality where there should be.

While Hideki Naganuma (the guy that made JSR's soundtrack) himself did contribute some songs to the game, the issue there is that there are also a bunch of indie music in the game that simply just don't sound like they belong in a JSR-like. That's one more thing about JSR, the whole soundtrack was composed by Naganuma, meaning he had full control over transitions and understood whether the songs meshed well in those transitions so that it didn't feel jarring when they change between each other. Here, you can tell whoever handled the audio in this game doesn't quite have that same understanding. They try... just not very well.

I feel like with all these foundational complaints however that I'm painting a bad picture. Is this game bad? No, in terms of gameplay, they did great capturing the feel JSR had. Sort of. They did have to take some liberties to make it work in some areas but overall they don't do a bad job of it. And while the story is kind of confusing and doesn't make a whole lot of sense in certain areas, JSR didn't exactly have an academy award winning story either so it's not like I can make that comparison fairly.

For those who just want a one-paragraph review: 7/10. A bit lacking but not necessarily bad. Definitely worth the full price for what it offers but reign those expectations if you're looking for something that encapsulates a modern-day Jet Set Radio game.

I never played [i]Jet Set Radio[/i], and so I almost dismissed [i]Bomb Rush Cyberfunk[/i] after the first hour. I'm glad I stuck with it. The first area is not very interesting or challenging, but the flow becomes really quite satisfying in some of the later levels. That said, I got this as part of my Humble Choice subscription and I would recommend waiting for a deep sale; the asking price is a bit steep for what it is.

I enjoyed this game! It has a lot of style and charm and the developers clearly put a lot of passion into it.

The art direction and style of the game is amazing. I love the Y2K aesthetic and everything in the game was just great to look at. The animation is really good too. The different skating and dancing animations are really well done and everything has a good weight and punches out at you.

The core gameplay of skating around and tagging things was fun, and it was always rewarding to get a new tag. I was a little disappointed, however, because I thought there was going to be more mechanical depth to the skating. It's very easy to just keep your combo going forever and I felt like I hit the skill ceiling halfway through the game. None of the challenges of having to beat the other crews or replicating tricks they did were difficult. It's still super fun to just vibe and skate around tagging things though, I just thought it was going to be a little deeper.

Combat was also very shallow and I wish it wasn't in the game, because all it did was make me want to be done with it as quickly as possible so I could get back to skating. The final boss was actually very fun though, because it didn't really use combat and instead made good use of the skating mechanics.

This is just personal preference, but the music was pretty hit or miss for me. A lot of the tracks were just very repetitive and just wasn't really my style.

The story is totally nonsensical and crazy. Not necessarily a bad thing, you just have to roll with the sillyness and you'll at least somewhat enjoy it haha.

This game is truly a great send up to Jet Set Radio and JSRF but for my 2 cents it misses some key things to really make it feel like it's own game. 

New Amsterdam... just doesn't feel distinct. I can't play a area and feel like i'm in a Dutch future city. It's feels more like an extension of Tokyo-to. Don't ask me what I would want because it would be hard for me to describe but... just some themeing in the various areas thaqt make this FEEL like a dutch city... not being dutch myself that's very hard to put into words for so, take that for what you will.

Second, when you conquer an area, by default, your crews music plays in that area. This takes away some of the individual area's identity. When i'm in the sewers in JSRF I hear The Scrappy, a song that more than FITS for the sewer area. when you go from one district to the next you do have similar tracks on the list but you also have tracks FOR THAT AREA. While the "non-discrpit neo city" critque still would have weight here it further exemplifys the problem of each area not truly having it's own personality. I'm NOT saying each doistrict isn't DISTINCT, just that they lose some that distinction when the area is conquered.

And finally... Where my prof. K man???? ok this is a minor gripe but a pirate DJ giving us lowdowns instead of reading what the characters say would be phenomenal.

Dispite that, this is a grand game and deserves a playthrough but with that distinct-ness missing... I don't feel compelled to come back to the game anytime soon... that makes me sad.

I got this game cause I saw mods and it was on sale, I didn't expect it to be as good as it is. 

It's obviously trying to evoke Jet Set Radio but I think it uses colour better and I think the characters are less blobby than the original Jet Set Radio. I think its implementation of cel shading is better and more convincing as well. The music is all surprisingly good, I know Naganuma did a few tracks, but all of them are pretty well done and high energy, the fades between tracks feel like you're listening to a DJ. It is missing an obnoxiously high energy announcer, but other than that it's very well done. The plot is also surprisingly well done in terms of story beats. I think they could have potentially added more, and maybe some subquests elaborate on the world a little bit, but I'm surprised about how tight this felt from beginning to end, with consistent thematics and character building and even an interesting (if callable) plot twist. It really feels like a decently produced game from the 2000s.

It isn't an extremely trying simulator game, opting more for a kind of easy going find-the-line gameplay loop. Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is a vibrant, high-energy love letter to the cult classic Jet Set Radio, yet it manages to carve out its own identity with a dazzling world, infectious soundtrack, and tight traversal mechanics. Developed by Team Reptile, this indie title thrives on style, attitude, and momentum, placing you in a futuristic cityscape where graffiti crews battle for turf while dodging militarized police and uncovering layers of mystery hidden in the neon-drenched streets. From the moment you dive in, the game bombards you with color, rhythm, and motion, inviting you into a kinetic playground that rewards creativity and precision in equal measure.

The story follows Red, a cybernetically enhanced graffiti artist seeking answers about his missing past while aiming to dominate the city’s graffiti scene. The narrative is intentionally pulpy and stylized, drawing from anime and hip-hop culture, mixing humor with moments of introspection. While the story isn’t overly deep or dramatic, it offers just enough structure to keep the action moving and lends some emotional weight to the crew dynamics and rivalries that unfold. Characters are over-the-top, cool in that ‘early 2000s rebellious youth’ kind of way, and they fit perfectly into the game’s larger-than-life tone.

Gameplay revolves around traversing the city with a mix of inline skating, BMX biking, and parkour, chaining tricks together while tagging designated graffiti spots across sprawling urban environments. The core loop is instantly satisfying: you gain points and speed by executing tricks, wall-riding, grinding, and flipping, all while maneuvering through a level design that encourages exploration and experimentation. The controls are responsive and smooth once you get the hang of them, and there’s a rhythm to chaining movements that gives the game a natural flow. It’s not just about flash—it’s about learning the terrain and moving through it like a skilled performer, turning the city into your canvas.

Each area in the game is packed with secrets, rival crews, and challenges, and the open-ended design encourages players to revisit zones with new abilities or tactics. Unlike traditional linear platformers, Bomb Rush Cyberfunk wants you to explore, improve, and master each corner of its map. Finding the best lines to maximize your trick combos or reach hard-to-tag areas gives the game a feeling of progression beyond simply unlocking new levels. Boss battles, rival crew face-offs, and hidden collectibles add layers of depth, keeping things fresh even after many hours of play.

Of course, a game like this lives or dies by its soundtrack, and Bomb Rush Cyberfunk absolutely delivers. The music is a diverse mix of funk, hip-hop, electronica, and experimental beats from both well-known artists like Hideki Naganuma (of Jet Set Radio fame) and a roster of indie musicians. Tracks blend perfectly with the visuals and gameplay, often matching the pace and tone of your movements as you cruise through back alleys, rooftops, and neon-lit railways. The sound design, from trick sounds to ambient city noise, complements the soundtrack without overwhelming it, and there’s a sense that every corner of the game world is alive with rhythm.

Visually, the game is a stunner. It uses cel-shading and bold color palettes to create a world that’s both futuristic and nostalgic, reminiscent of the Dreamcast era but brought into the modern age. Character designs are stylish and expressive, and each city zone has its own identity—ranging from sleek downtown areas to gritty industrial zones. The art direction embraces exaggeration, from the over-the-top animations to the stylized graffiti tags that explode with personality when painted. It’s a joy to simply exist in this world, let alone blaze through it doing tricks.

On the downside, there are a few moments where the camera can be finicky, especially in tight interior areas or while navigating vertical sections. There’s also a learning curve for those unfamiliar with trick-based movement systems—timing, momentum, and positioning are essential, and some players may struggle early on. Additionally, the combat system, though functional, feels underdeveloped compared to the rest of the game, with most encounters being little more than minor interruptions in your flow. These issues don’t seriously detract from the overall experience but are worth noting.

Ultimately, Bomb Rush Cyberfunk succeeds because it knows exactly what it wants to be: a celebration of movement, music, and rebellion. It taps into the spirit of a subculture often ignored by mainstream games, creating a world that feels both nostalgic and forward-thinking. For fans of Jet Set Radio, it’s a spiritual successor that finally fills the void left behind. For newcomers, it’s a wildly creative and exhilarating ride through a world where self-expression and style are your greatest weapons. It’s not just about tagging walls—it’s about leaving your mark on a world that dares you to keep moving.

I'm glad I stuck with the game though. 

BRC opens up after the first few hours, evolving from a simple skateboard game to Tony Hawk Underground with deep environmental exploration components. The story also becomes oddly gripping as the designers imagine an urban cyberpunk police state where the arts clash with the government. Stakes quickly become grandiose. 

My one major criticism is that the tricks in BCR feel simple. Unlike Tony Hawk you don't have to do button combos to pull off tricks. Every trick you can perform is tied to a single button. However, the tricks aren't the true core of the game... it's the level design and platforming.  The game is at its best as you try to figure out how to get to some obscure spot to hit a gang tag as you rock out the game's excellent soundtrack in its lush, urban artstyle.

I must say, as a fan of Jet Set Radio, I was eagerly looking forward to Bomb Rush Cyberfunk, waiting to feel those same feelings again and have the same experience but fresh and anewed. I was waiting for Hideki Naganuma, who I thought fully responsible for the OST of the game, to fill my ears, but found out rather swiftly the disparity between the two games was larger than expected.

The game featured an array of artists on its OST that were not the expected and awaited Hideki songs, but many others with varying tone and colour, bringing different aesthetics into the levels and gameplay atmosphere with them. Some of them I honestly disliked, some of them I felt indifferent about, but a few I found enjoyable and reminiscent of what I was looking for, putting me in the right mood to make it an enjoyable experience as the game let me choose what songs i wished to listen to.

The story itself was surprisingly well thought out and, although it leans on some of the preconceived ideas from Jet Set Radio, it does manage to set itself apart from its predecessor in bringing us a story with more character involvement and progression, leading to higher investment into them. Of course, the depth of this was still limited due to it being a skating/BMX/roller-skating game, but I still felt they managed to bring it to a good middle ground where it led through the levels nicely without interfering with the gameplay. I did, however, feel like many of the cutscenes felt static and lacking, and could have stood to be more emotive and full of motion.

Gameplay itself felt rather good. The rails felt snappy, the controls over your character feel good, but I'd have wished for some more elaborate and in-depth stunts or combos to be present to really challenge oneself more within the game's levels—hoping they'd go as in-depth as the graffiti art system implemented within the game, which sports many great pieces you can tag any wall with, whichever way you choose and feel fitting within the world and its overarching art direction, which I found no faults with.

Overall a good game I'd recommend.

I loved the movement and tricking systems, for the entirety of my ~20 hours, including after the story to snag all the achievements, I found myself taking long parkour routes just so I could spend more time doing tricks and watching the sweet animations. Everything was really fluid and it felt [i]good[/i] to string together huge combos for points. I simply [b]loved[/b] how the phone + camera works. Seeing the character's head glued to the screen if you're trying to check the map while moving was entertaining. I even tried playing phone games while high-speed tricking. [spoiler]It didn't go well. Remember to never text and parkour.[/spoiler] 

The story was alright, a few twists and turns to keep things interesting, but nothing to knock your socks off. I will say that I liked the feeling of the individual characters, they kept a strong sense of personality throughout the story.

The combat I would say was the game's weakest point. It was a button spam fest with some small variations on the later enemies. I was really left wanting when some of the bigger boys showed up to be killed faster than a group of the most basic ones. However, I will say that I don't care too much since it was weak in the direction of being easy. I really just wanted to spend more time doing tricks, and that's what I got.

The soundtrack was pretty sweet all throughout. It really solidified the skater vibe throughout and I felt myself doing tricks and planning my route to the tempo of whatever was playing. The art was also stylised in a consistent way, I would've liked to see a bit more variation with some of the NPCs beyond the main cast, but the character design was solid for them. Loved some of the graffiti designs.

Overall, [b]7.5/10[/b]. Great fun game, give it a shot if you're looking for something funky fresh.

No matter what I accomplish in my life, I regret that I cannot say I came up with the single greatest title for a video game ever: "Bomb Rush Cyberfunk."

A triumph! This was my introduction to the gang/graffiti/parkour platformer genre and what a way to start! So no, for reference, I have not played the *Jet Set Radio* games yet, so I can't compare this obvious spiritual successor to those. But man, what a ride!

I've had my eye on Team Reptile since *Lethal League* - a superb unique fighting/sports game. Throw in Hideki Naganuma's music and I had to play this. And yes, even if you only play for the soundtrack it might be worth your time. A compilation of electronic funk songs from an eclectic array of composers that makes the entire game just one solid continuous vibe. Add addictive platforming and tricking gameplay with collectathon elements, a genuinely perfect cel-shaded artstyle, and tight controls and the game really does exceed the sum of its relatively small development team.

If I had to nitpick, there were a few frustrating segments - particularly any time combat is involved. Combat never feels as tight or responsive as the skate controls and bosses are relatively simple and uninspired. That's really all the negatives I have for it, though.

World building and narrative were shockingly...uh...present? I don't know why I wasn't expecting much of a story, but there is one here. It's not the best story ever, but it's solid enough and even tries to pull off some ambitious twists and turns that mostly work. Rival gangs are unique and honestly hilarious. And the game knows exactly how serious it needs to be, striking a perfect balance between cyberpunk absurdity and serious stakes.

Do yourself a favor and play *Bomb Rush Cyberfunk.*

Combat is perhaps the weakest part of the game, but you do this pretty minimally. Boss fights were easier than the challenges. There is a nitpick I have related to gameplay and that has to do with traversal gimmicks. 
 [list]

[h3] Story [/h3]

When I firsts started playing it I went "Man, this feels like playing a new Dreamcast in 2025", and it is!  But it's unfortunately for both good and bad reasons.  It has a fantastic visual style and sense of audio-visual aesthetics that makes me want to spend time in it, but totally fumbles the bag when it comes to level design and basic modern design conveniences, and will constantly get in it's own way of the fun.

The stunt and combo mechanics are fun and a meaningful improvement over it's predecessor (Jet Set Radio Future), and they make me want to just play around, but most of these future city environments feel simultaneously cavernous, empty and weirdly linear for a game about trying to combo tricks and they feel less fun to navigate.  And just when I'm getting info a flow with the game it has this bad old-school cutscene system where triggering events will yank the camera away from what you're doing just to highlight a basic level event like the cops appearing or where to go next, when they could have indicated that to me from my character's perspective like any other modern game in the last 10-15 years will do.

And then there's the janky stuff that just feels straight out of the old Jet Set Radio/Future games, like the boring police combat, bad forced camera angles during certain boss fights (big Sonic Adventure vibes here),  the awkwardly sequenced audio and the static cutscenes that don't do much to add life to the story that peaks 10 minutes in.

If you like what you see from the videos then you'll probably enjoy it and I did have fun here, I think i'm just disappointed that 22 years after Jet Set Radio Future this game doesn't feel like it makes the leap forward it should have.

In all seriousness this review is coming from a huge fan of Jet Set Radio Future 


Let’s start with the good: 

The tricks and smoothness of movement in this game are amazing. I think that they knocked that out of the park. Not to mention that you don’t have to just stick to skating. I also really enjoyed that the graffiti mechanics and being able to do different designs at any time is awesome. These are honestly improvements over the original games. 

The graphics and level designs are spot on and pay homage to the original. I really enjoyed Red’s mind levels. It makes me wish there was a level editor so fans can make their own maps and share them with each other.

Overall, these are the elements that do the game justice and make this a very good predecessor of the Jet Set franchise. 

The story was pretty good. It has some mystery elements to it that I enjoyed. The instrumental music tracks went hard! The Japanese track was my favorite.  


Now onto the Bad: 

So personally, I did not like a lot of the music. Much of it was very repetitive and not catchy. I think making lyric heavy music was a mistake as the instrumental tracks are the ones that shined. 

Not having a limited number of graffiti cans made tagging and combat too easy. And thus, I would never go out of my way to get the booster balls because you get them by just playing normally. 

The combat was very boring in my opinion. All you have to do is spam on enemies, and you don’t even need to spray them to beat them. The boss battles were just as easy as the main enemies as well. The most interesting boss was DJ Cyber and even he was too easy. DJ Cyber was the only boss I died to. 

Also crew battles where the same exact thing over and over. There was nothing unique or fun about those. All you have to do is hit corners and Cressy Slide over and over and you can beat every crew battle first try. 


Final Thoughts: 

The Ticks, Art style, and music do make this game worthwhile to play if you want to feel a bit of nostalgia and have been craving another Jet Set Radio Future game. 

However, they took 1 step forward and 2 steps back by making this game is far too easy and repetitive. Making this a one and done type of game where I will most likely not be replaying anytime soon. 

I would still buy this game and play it, but I would personally wait for a sale.


To the developers:

I get this is a different game from Jet Set Radio & Jet Set Radio Future. But I personally would have added more elements from the original games that made them so fun. I.e limited graffiti cans, ability to make custom graffiti designs, add variation to crew battles with different objectives, making it f so you have to spray enemies to kill them, and just make the game more difficulty.

The only significant issue is the often unclear mission guidance, particularly in chapter where u need to find a doctor to save the protagonist. Below is my solution:
1. The 1st gang member can be found riding a bicycle near the connector between Mataan and Millennium Square (on the map, this appears as a narrow, protruding pathway extending from the plaza).
2. After following the instructions to Brink Terminal, head to the elevated half-pipe structure ahead.
3. The third one is located on the 'under' horizontal highway after entering Mataan overpass, then proceed to the underground passage where a low vent leads to a small basketball court.
Additionally, the game has known savefile issues, including occasional corruption or failure to unlock collectibles in the statistics. If you don't have moral reservations about modifying saves, you may search for an open-source project called brc-save-editor, which allows you to unlock relevant options via a web interface.

After waiting for it since its very first teaser and initially playing it on Switch, I finally bought it again on Steam. Team Reptile managed to capture and enhance both the gameplay and aesthetic of Jet Set Radio Future. Just like with Lethal League, they added a strong dose of personality and elevated the formula even further.

I’ve seen some comments saying the game feels repetitive. With three years of hindsight and a more objective perspective, it's true that a certain sense of repetition can emerge, especially from performing similar actions in each new area. That said, the platforming segments in Red’s dreams are very engaging. I would have loved to see that level of challenge in the regular platforming zones or boss fights. The game is much more vertical than its predecessors, though it’s not exactly a hardcore platformer.

Once you understand that it's the corners and the signs that grant multipliers, and you’re playing through the game for the third or fourth time, the difficulty drops significantly — which makes sense, since you’ve mastered it by then. Still, it would be interesting to see the difficulty curve rethought for a potential sequel, to keep things engaging for more experienced players.

All that may sound negative, but if you’re playing the game for the first time, the gameplay is so satisfying that you likely won’t even notice this potential repetitiveness. The colors, environments, characters, story, and especially the music immerse you in a rich and highly creative universe.

The game's overall atmosphere alone is enough to make you love its content and what it has to offer. Mods further enhance the experience by adding new content, unique experiences, and great fixes. Sort the mods by popularity on Thunderbolt, and you’ll find some really cool stuff to check out after just a few hours of play.

I sincerely recommend playing this game. I waited for it as a spiritual successor to Jet Set Radio Future, and I was absolutely not disappointed. It’s a game I love, and one I regularly come back to — especially to play online with friends. Go for it!!!

Bomb Rush Cyberfunk doesn't particularly do anything new, it basically tries to do what jet set radio did back in the day while trying to modernise controls and other QOL stuff, and I can't say it bothers me because this game is really fun.

[h2]Gameplay [/h2]
BRC has a very basic structure, get to a new aera, graph a few walls, challenge the local gang, get in a big "challenge", gain the territory as a reward. All of that with a lot of story in between, but the main fun of the game is controlling your character and doing bigall combos. The game felt pretty easy throughout it's total length, all the challenges aren't really hard and encourage more of a layed back exploration style of gameplay than an hardcore scoring arcade type of gameplay, but it's def very fun to explore the new aeras and try to get all the little collectibles and secrets here and there.

[h2]Graphics and overall Presentation [/h2]
This is where the game really hits the spot for me, the overall artistic direction, music, the overall vibe of the game is FANTASTIC (I Wanna Know by Two Mellow will probably be my most listened tune this year). The overall design of the aeras and character designs really hits the spot for me and for that alone I recommand playing this game!

[h1]Conclusion [/h1]
Bomb Rush Cyberfunk feels like a more modern and more accessible Jet Set Radio, and while i would of liked a little more challenge, the game is still fantastic!

I have a lot I could say about this so I'll keep it as brief as I can. This is good! One of the highest recommendations I'll give for something I played this year.

But I'm not gonna lie, I think there's a lot of factors that make it good to me specifically, that I think the average person might not be as into:

First of all, elephant in the room, the entire style of this game is insane. Every aspect of the game is curated to a specific "y2k" aesthetic that I am absolutely obsessed with. All of the art, all of the music, every detail is incredibly on point. To the degree that this genuinely feels like it could have released in 2004 or something, which is both a positive and negative, but I think is definitely what they were going for. 

Second, in terms of gameplay, the thing I can compare it most to (other than Jet Set Radio, which it's of course connected to), is Tony Hawk's Pro Skater, another game I famously enjoy a lot haha.

Just to rattle off some negatives though - All of the songs are great, but there's only about 20-25 of them in the game, so you end up hearing a lot of them over and over in an 11 hour playthrough. Additionally, some of the gameplay feels a liiiitle jank, which kind of plays into the 'feeling like it came out in 2004' factor. This could potentially be a skill issue I guess if you wanted to be lame but it just made some sections of the platforming feel very unsatisfying when you miss one step and lose like minutes of progress.

There's objectively a story here which is honestly interesting enough to work for me but the "voice acting," if you could even call it that, makes it a little more difficult to get into.

All in all, I think this is absolutely worth a play because it's so very singular in every aspect, but it wouldn't be winning anyone's GOTY awards or anything

This is a tricky one. As a Jet Set Radio Future obsessive, and later, Jet Set Radio, (the two left-field rollerblading, spraying, future-grinding games that Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is a direct homage to), I put off playing this for a bit. The possibility of disappointment was too great! But turns out this is a super fun game that kept me plugged in, and not just because of mis-placed nostalgia. That said, it has a high bar to live up to, and I don't think it quite clears it.

The start of this game is a goddamn slog. The game *does* have fun characters, but they sure aren't around at the start. The starting areas are drab and the cut-scenes are SLOW. The music hadn't grown on me at this stage, and I was pretty mad that they didn't just get 2 Mello (absolutely jammin' JSR-style music producer) to do the whole soundtrack. And skateboards? This is a goofy game, and having "cool" skateboards and bikes (with no futuristic add-ons) is jarring. For the first couple of hours I was having a pretty grumpy - but not terrible - time. I was sure that it was going to be nostalgia that pulled me through.

Then, not too far in, the game opened up, I'm unlocking tags, new areas, and hooking together combos like nobody's business. There are improvements in this game! The tag system is great. The flip-phone map and camera system is GENIUS. The cut-scenes are still boring, but you get to meet a claustrophobic masochist, who is always in tight spaces having a terribly good time. The police enemies are annoying (on brand for JSR). The main thing is that the flow is gooooood. I maintain that some of the level design is very poor, with some unlockables requiring specific backtracking or annoying hidden access points, but if you find yourself going for the unlockables and achievements that require combos, you will be in for a treat as you start to flow through the large levels. The soundtrack grew on me, and I have the soundtrack LP on order...

Overall, an incredible achievement. The team put this together with a lot of love, and without a big budget. Nailing the look, getting the soundtrack together, the tags, the amount of characters... an absolute lifetime achievement. It's not perfect, but I'll be damned if I would give this a thumbs down - if only because I want Bomb Rush Cyberfunk Future so badly! Get this, and get the Jet Set Radio remaster, and fall in love with a absolutely unique vibe.

Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is a terrific game—from the world to the characters and especially the music. The game is a true callback to that early 2000s feel, and I love everything about it.

The gameplay is fun and engaging, and the combo system lets you experiment and find new ways to pull off huge combos. With the OST banging in your ears, that's all the motivation you’ll need. Surprisingly, the story is really good. Going into the game, I didn’t expect the story to take center stage, but it ended up being a huge factor in my engagement.

The only real downside is one of the activities in the story. The squad battles are fun and make sense within the narrative, but I just wish there was more variety. It’s always just about who gets the highest combo, and it's really easy to win.

And then there’s the heat system. The system itself is fine—it’s basically like getting a wanted level in GTA—but the problem is the cutscenes you have to watch EVERY. SINGLE. TIME. It gets old fast, and even skipping them isn’t fast enough.

Other than that, I think everything about this game is great, and I really hope they continue it with a sequel.

[b]Bomb Rush Cyberfunk[/b]
33 hours on record — and every single second was a masterpiece of style, color, and pure [b]vibes[/b].

This game… THIS GAME! It’s everything I wanted and more. I love it so much I got my brothers and cousins to play it right after I finished. The moment I jumped into the world, the music hit, the moves flowed, and the graffiti sprayed — I knew I was home again.

As a [b]Jet Set Radio[/b] and [b]JSRF[/b] fan, this game gave me that same rush of nostalgia, attitude, and rhythm that defined an era. [b]Bomb Rush Cyberfunk[/b] doesn’t just copy the old formula — it evolves it, amplifies it, and delivers it with a cyber-soul that screams love for the genre. The machines, the tricks, the city — it’s all beautiful chaos done right.

The [b]world design[/b] is insane. The city of New Amsterdam feels alive, full of personality and funk. The graffiti system is satisfying, the music is pure fire, and the controls just feel buttery smooth. Every borough had its own flavor, and I couldn’t stop exploring.

The [b]story[/b] was surprisingly heartfelt too — Red’s journey was weird, cool, and emotional in its own way. I genuinely didn’t expect to be that invested in a guy with a cyberhead and a dream, but here we are.

If I had one small complaint, it’s that I wish there was [b]multiplayer[/b]. Imagine rolling around with your crew tagging walls together — that would’ve been legendary. But even without it, this game is perfection in motion.

It’s stylish, funky, rebellious, and unforgettable. I’ll say it again for the people in the back: [b]THIS GAME UNDERSTOOD THE CONCEPT OF LOVE![/b]

In order to properly communicate the quality of this game, I am going to break this review up into three parts: gameplay without mods, gameplay with mods, story, and miscellaneous. Keep in mind that there are minor spoilers throughout this review.

[h3] Gameplay(without mods) [/h3]
If you are familiar with any of the Jet Set Radio games or even some of the Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater games, then you will most likely enjoy this game even more. The general premise is that you move around big open areas using either a skateboard, bike, or inline skates. With any of these tools, your goal is to perform tricks and combos, grind rails, wall ride, and spray graffiti to achieve a high score.

In each of these big open areas, your goal is to participate in challenges, solo score battles, and team battles to claim that respective area as your territory. Along the way, you will encounter various enemies, such as different types of police officers and machinery, which you will need to defeat. This structure continues until you face the final boss, concluding the main story. Afterward, there is a decent amount of post-game content, which involves completing more score battles in previously visited areas.

In general, the movement feels really good, especially if you’re familiar with Jet Set Radio. One thing to note about the movement is that it feels very balanced. On one hand, this makes the game approachable for new players, as there’s a slight learning curve. On the other hand, the balanced movement system may feel repetitive for players who have mastered it and want a more skill-based, exciting experience. Overall, the gameplay in its vanilla state works perfectly fine and doesn’t require any changes.

[h3] Gameplay(with mods) [/h3]
Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is lucky to have a large library of mods available. Unfortunately, there are far too many mods to cover here, so I’ll highlight the "must-have" mods and the ones I personally had the most fun with.

The three must-have mods, in my opinion, are CrewBoom, DripRemix, and BombRushRadio. These mods allow you to change player models, add more characters, swap out your equipment on the fly, and add your own music, making the experience feel more personal.

Some mods that I personally enjoyed include MovementPlus, WallPlant, and MapStation. Without getting too detailed, MovementPlus and WallPlant enhance speed and mobility, while MapStation is the main mod for adding new maps to the game. One caveat with MovementPlus is that it causes non-cop CPU characters to behave strangely. However, this isn’t a big deal if you’re using the mod post-game.

Overall, mods turn this game into a playground, making the experience much more enjoyable. You won’t have a bad time playing the game with mods, especially if you’re looking for something more from the gameplay.

[h3] Story [/h3]
I’m not going to explain the story in detail, as I’d be here all day, but I’ll give my thoughts on it.

When I played through the game for the first time, I found the story weird and confusing. However, I’ll admit that this might have been because I wasn’t paying enough attention. On my second playthrough, I enjoyed the story much more. As you progress, the game slowly reveals the main conflict in one of the most creative ways I’ve seen in a while. It constantly throws twists at you, keeping you unsure of what will happen next.

In the end, the story delivers a solid final message that anyone can relate to and apply to their own life. Overall, the story can be hard to follow at times, but it’s really solid once you understand what’s happening.

[h3] Miscellaneous [/h3]
There are a couple of small things worth mentioning here.

First, the soundtrack is fantastic. Individual tracks can be unlocked as collectibles, along with specific mixtapes that play automatically depending on what part of the game you’re in. These mixtapes do a great job of establishing the energy of the rival team or the area where they’re located.

I was especially happy to see Hideki Naganuma return to contribute a few tracks, as his music perfectly matches the game’s energy.

Other collectibles include extra bikes, skates, skateboards, and graffiti. Most of these are appropriately tricky to collect, though some require specific equipment (skates, bikes, or skateboards) to access. This can get a little annoying when you need to switch to a character with the required equipment. Fortunately, mods can fix this, so it didn’t bother me during my second playthrough.

[h3] Conclusion [/h3]
To wrap this up, this game is excellent. Gameplay is solid, story is interesting, and music is very good. I would also consider this game to be very user-friendly as well as computer friendly, as you really don't need an excellent computer to run this game. On an unrelated note, this is the only game so far where I wanted to give a legit review, as my other review are either ironic or short. So to end this review, I'm going to rate the first three sections.

Belonging to a vibration that hasn't vibrated since 2002, Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is the returning heartbeat of a genre that still doesn't exist. 

Team Reptile digs up the unaltered remains of Jet Set Radio with reverence and confidently pieces them back together into something new and improved. Yet the timeless spirit of it's predecessor still remains. The funky soul of this video game was so potent that I had to check my diaper every 5 minutes to see if the stank was emanating from me. If the gameplay was less engaging you'd probably get hung up on the idea that the lead composer just shitted. Your inner child will be cheering for big jumps on a skateboard while you sit back with a fancy tobacco pipe, monocle resting on your face, admiring the calligraphy.  

The biggest sin of this game is not giving us more. The good news is, if the release pattern of this type of game is future accurate; then we are guaranteed to receive a spiritual successor with a similar 3-word naming convention by a different studio in 20~ years time. Bomb Rush Cyberfunk belongs in a museum alongside Jet Set Radio and by the time we get a sequel,  I will be the decrepit janitor wiping down it's display glass.

Fantastic game. Some quirks here and there with side progression (some quests where you spray graffiti at the end give you rep, others don't), but otherwise great gameplay and aesthetically pleasing environments. I especially love the Millennium Mall and Brink Terminal. Character customization is fun and I love getting to choose between different movestyles and color schemes.

Exploration is heavily encouraged throughout the game thanks to all the unlockables and hidden items. The story is a bit easy, but the side content and achievements make up for it.

I think the game would benefit from a secret unlockable level that is very hard. Maybe they could add one as dlc for after story mode is finished? I'd totally go for it.

For context, I have loved Jet Set Radio back during the pandemic, and was able to let JSR sit in the back of my mind. With that, I can say that Bomb Rush Cyberfunk manages to perfectly grab all the aesthetic from it's spiritual predecessor while also building on the style established in the Lethal League Blaze. 

As for the game play, it has a flow with mechanics that helps amplify the base mechanics flow, one of the best additions being the manual. The slide allows you to grind or slide across the ground for a little at the press of the button, which helps recover your combo if you accidentally over or undershoot the rails. The boost pack is also one of these amplifying mechanics as it allows either for you to make a jump you couldn't have made otherwise, or speeding up your rail grind. Graffiti's new system not only allows for the option to have multiple different graffiti in the level, but also has a more understandable way to scale graffiti difficulty compared to Jet Set's string of random stick inputs.

However I do have some negative viewpoints, such as I feel that voice acting could've really enhanced the story as it's low poly art style with textured faces didn't allow visuals to truly enhance the dialog. While I did praise the graffiti systems understandable difficulty scaling, I feel there isn't a reason to get good at graffiti scaling besides getting back to skating, as the slider that kicks you out of the graffiti screen is so slow. There is also the fact the game fails to properly explain to you some hidden mechanics, from small things like manual time affected by speed, to some important things like combo multipliers not being applied when you lean into a corner while doing a trick.

All in all, this game is a great follow up to it's spiritual processor Jet Set Radio, while also expanding into an identity of it's own. I would say it is worth the price point. As although the story is short, there is definitely replay-ability weather it is every few years or bi annually.

Spiritual succesors are by definition titles that want to capture the essence, style, the spirit and what made it 'tick' to back in the day. Sometimes they sell it short, trying to capture what the original did but at the same time not improving on set formula or even worse; not being able resonate with  the target audience nor expands its horizons to find new public either, eventually getting stuck in an identity limbo. Others delivers exactly what it promises, knows what made the original game special while still not evolving its core concepts; serving as an alternative to the original source. Then, there exists rare cases where its spiritual succesor goes far and beyond what was originally did. Improving in every single aspect it was meant to achieve, probably even replacing and surprasing its inspiration. Where does [i] Bomb Rush Cyberfunk[/i] falls exactly? We'll see.

As you may know, [i] Bomb Rush Cyberfunk[/i] is one of the few alternatives we have to [i] Jet Set Radio[/i] nowdays. [i] Bomb Rush Cyberfunk[/i] feels modern in a sense that is actually easier for people to get their hands on it, being more accesible than ever thanks to it being avaible to purchase in a wide arrange of different platforms and stores. In comparasion to the unfortunate legacy of [i] Jet Set Radio[/i] which is digitally stuck on the Xbox 360, PlayStation 3/Vita era and now being delisted from Steam. [i] Jet Set Future [/i] ran into a worse outcome, as it was an exclusive to a console and hasn't seen a re-release ever since, even if the Xbox Team actually pushed the idea to at least be more accesible on their current systems. It's a shame because I, myself haven't played any single *Jet Set Radio* game prior to this review and the only avaible game on the series.. This pushed me to play B.R.C, as I wanted a modern, future-proof alternative to [i] Jet Set Radio[/i].

[i] Bomb Rush Cyberfunk[/i] basically is an arcade-like sports game where the objective is...to have fun! Accumulate points by grinding walls, rails, performing air tricks and turbo-through your way to the top of a turf war. It is simple, in a way little to nothing really tries to get in your way and the game actively encourages to not stop this grindfest, unless you said so. There are 7 maps including the Hideout, each representing seven different crews you'll have to face throughout the story. Each crew have their unique style, moveset, music and even dance moves. This extends to the city they are set in as well. Most crews more or less act as rivals the Bomb Rush Cyberfunk crew has to beat in order to advance to the next turf, be it through challenges or gaining enough REP in each district.                       

About the story, it's surprisnlgly entertaining and darker than I originally expected to be. So, you're basically this guy called Red, he loses his 'head' during an accident, in the most literal sense and we're set to recover it. The game doesn't goes to show 'that' accident, as it is story about how everything hapenned, what events led to that moment. There are instances that can feel boring when there isn't further variation in what the player actually does, it's like playing with cheats on. Too easy, no challenge

Ultimately, the game doesn't live up to the hype, and I'd rather spend my time playing JSRF or some other game.

Underwhelming spiritual successor to Jet Set Radio.

While I may not be the biggest Jet Set Radio fan out there, I still find it to be a pretty fun action/platform game. And when I saw that someone was going to create a Jet Set Radio style game for the modern age, I did get quite excited. However, having dipped my toes into the game now, I feel rather disappointed.

The movement in Bomb Rush Cyberfunk feels noticeably worse than what Jet Set Radio offered. And I think that's a two-pronged issue, one part being controls and one part being level design. On the control side, I had trouble getting my character to control as I wish. Feels like the characters can cut far too sharp in a direction when coming from a jump, and like it happens in an unpredictable fashion. And the control issues are not helped by the fact that the controls are more intricate than Jet Set Radio's, with many more movement possibilities. I could've taken less if the counterbalance was that it felt more intuitive to move.

And the early levels feel very sparse in comparison to Jet Set Radio with large open areas without any parts for grinding or jumping. In Jet Set Radio, if you saw a ramp going upwards, you could most likely grind against it. But in Bomb Rush Cyberfunk, it feels like I was constantly trying to grind against level elements that just didn't support it. And having to second-guess what parts of the level work for movement and which don't really kills the flow. The levels really didn't feel like they were designed to allow for stylishly combining various tricks to your heart's contents as long as you had the skills. Maybe I'd learn the movement controls in due time but I'm not sure if the level design would ever allow the same kind of free-flowing movement that Jet Set Radio had.

The approach to levels seems very different between the two. Jet Set Radio would throw you into a level with a map of all tag locations and big honking arrows pointing to the tags inside the game. Bomb Rush Cyberfunk meanwhile throws you into a map without any tag locations, no arrows and tells you to go spray enough of them to unlock the next objective. Jet Set Radio was more of a time attack whereas Bomb Rush Cyberfunk seems to be more of an exploration. And I don't think exploration really meshes well with the kind of movement-based gameplay associated with Jet Set Radio.

After I managed to clear the first couple of reputation gates by spraying tags, the gameplay really slowed down as I was now just trying to hunt down any tags I'd missed instead of doing stylish grinds and jumps towards my next objective. The only way to tell apart done and undone tags is with this small shimmering effect on top of the sprays, which is much harder to spot in movement. The minimap would only show you the location of the reputation gate, which would angrily send you back because you hadn't done enough spraying yet. You can't even use the spray button prompt to figure out if you've done a tag, since for some reason you can spray the same tag multiple times. As far as I could tell, there was no benefit in doing so, but it was for some reason still possible.

The spraying itself also makes little sense. Jet Set Radio showed you exactly what kind of joystick movements you should do, and if you screwed up the sequence of moves, you'd lose valuable spray paint and would need to go collect more. Here, you seem to be able to just wiggle the joystick around for about a second and you're done. No sense of accomplishment for a job well done, no punishment for spraying with your eyes closed. At least I was never able to screw up a single tag by just wiggling my joystick around without paying attention. You might as well just have the spraying happen automatically.

Bomb Rush Cyberfunk also differs from its spiritual forefather by having a combat system. A combat system that doesn't really feel fun. You might be thrown into a stage with a handful of mob cops and one flying cop, who will fly around and then deliver you heaven's punishment from above. And the game doesn't really feel like giving you any helping hand to figuring out where this flying cop is relative to your position, making it much harder to dodge the incoming attacks. And trying to take down the flying cop is also painful due to lacking any kind of a lock-on system, which seems like something a game throwing many opponents at you at once should have. And even when you are successfully taking down your opponents, it doesn't feel satisfying. More like just some flailing around. If the combat was completely optional, maybe in the style of Mirror's Edge, I might give it a pass, but as far as I can tell, some combat sections are not optional.

The combat sections also seem to suffer from the same lack of direction as the spraying part of the game. I got thrown into a combat section, and I didn't really know what was my objective. Should I just outrun and escape the cops? Should I beat up every single cop coming my way? Or should I just focus on the flying cop that was in the cutscene? Once again, the only direction that the game seemed to be telling me was "go earn more reputation". Guidance that was not really helpful when I was being hunted by the jetpack police.

The game does very much pull off the Jet Set Radio style. It does very much look like it was just another Jet Set Radio game released on the Dreamcast, for better and for worse. But while the graphics do look old, it is a very functional design. That was probably to be expected considering how well Jet Set Radio has aged. I might not like the levels from a gameplay perspective, I did enjoy them from an aesthetics perspective. Just maybe if they weren't as empty-feeling. Soundtrack seemed fine too, although it doesn't rival Jet Set Radio in the sound department. Then again, really no game can.

I really would've liked to love this game, but I don't think I can as it is. For the 40-euro price tag, it feels pretty underwhelming and undercooked. Some of the issues I had with the game could probably be improved, but I'm not sure if the core gameplay could be improved to a degree that made this feel like worth its price tag. Perhaps once it hits the bargain bin, I might give it another chance.

I approached this game with genuine enthusiasm, truly wanting to embrace it. However, I find myself struggling. The combat feels clunky, the narrative lacks sufficient depth, and the movement, while passable, is far from exceptional. It's not a terrible game, but rather a decidedly mediocre experience. I'm genuinely perplexed by the overwhelmingly positive reception on Steam. Perhaps it's fueled by nostalgia for old games, a sentiment I don't share. At best, it's an 'okay' game. As a Humble Choice recipient, I'm left somewhat underwhelmed.

When games like Yooka Laylee or Armikrog pop up wanting to cash in on the fondness of an old franchise, fail to meet the standard set by their predecessors, and gets absolutely lambasted for it, I'm utterly baffled as to how this game ended up with an overwhelmingly positive rating instead.
The graphics are pretty and screenshots look like they could've come right out of JSRF, but that's all the positive things I can say about this.
The inundation of cutscenes is exhausting on top of being poorly presented, with characters just standing around blankly as they have no idle animations or facial expressions. The writing is downright amateurish and certainly couldn't get me to care about any of these characters. JSRF at least had some major characters be voice acted in cutscenes, here you don't even get that, you just get a handful of grunts at best.

Everyone disliked the tutorial segments in JSR and JSRF for being excessively long, but this game's tutorialisation period is even worse.  There are multiple boss fights early on too, each more awful to play through than the last.
But the worst crime the game commits is a complete lack of momentum in movement; you move at a slower speed on foot and a faster speed when on your ride, that's it, going downhill doesn't speed you up, going uphill doesn't slow you down, at best you can hold down a button to boost at a slightly faster speed or tap a different button for an instant direction change + speed boost once in the air. Everything about the movement here feels wrong, it's stilted, it's artificial, you touch a halfpipe and immediately shoot out at max speed, it's totally busted. The only bit of praise I can give it is that you boost your speed and combos by turning into corners when grinding, but this also means that combo scores are focused primarily on grind rails at the expense of other tricks, one thing you'd think they wouldn't copy from JSRF.
Adding to the lack of momentum is the graffiti system where you have to stop at every point to do a stick waggling minigame for each tag. JSR had this, but not for the smallest ones, and JSRF got rid of it to match the design being open world instead of stage and routing based. BRC brings it back, and the small ones don't have the minigame but still pause your movement to display the tag, so every tag completely breaks the flow. The game's areas are also huge and full of empty space, probably because they wanted to make the manual tricks have more purpose, but as a result the locations are just boring to look at and boring to explore.

Making matters even worse is the soundtrack, in the entire time I played there was only one decent song which was of course Naganuma's track that they used in all the advertising, while everything else ranged from dull to downright annoying. It wasn't as bad as Birthday Cake but some tracks damn near came close.

This just feels like another game that completely missed the mark of what it was trying to copy, and for the price they're charging you'd expect it to have much higher production values than it does. I'm just disappointed, man.

Jet Set Radio had a few arcade modes, like a time trial for getting a high trick score, or my favorite: seeing how fast you can tag all the graffiti spots. [h2]Not Worth The Price[/h2]
Bombrush CyberFunk is a pretty decent game, I’ll give them that. Growing up, I didn’t get to play a lot of games, but the ones I did were classics like Spyro, Jet Set Radio, Tony Hawk, and others. It was a time when gaming brought people together, where you’d sit around in the living room, engage with one another, and bond over music, high-score combos, and the challenge of seeing who could get the highest score. Those were the moments that made gaming meaningful, and what mades games like this more fun to actually play through.

What makes Bombrush Cyberfunk hard to recommend is the lack of deep, engaging gameplay. As someone who’s played similar games in the past, I can’t help but feel that it falls short. I don’t base my opinion on ratings; I focus on the game itself. While everyone has their own views, I believe this game is being overhyped and often misrepresented on social media as something it’s not.

[h2]Issues[/h2]
Again, this is all just personal opinion. Half of the soundtrack in Bombrush Cyberfunk consists of tracks I’ve heard thousands of times through various playlists, sometimes even mistaking them for songs from Jet Set Radio. While there are definitely some great tracks when they actually play, there’s also a fair amount of annoying music. On top of that, the game suffers from poor optimization. In fact, to get the full experience, you’d be better off downloading community mods to enhance the game, like the music mod that lets you actually select and organize your own playlists. Otherwise, you’ll be stuck hearing the same repetitive track, “LET ME SEE YOU SHAKE THAT AS-AS-AS-AS-AS-AS-AS” for the hundredth time in the early stages. There’s an equal mix of great songs and downright irritating ones.

This genre doesn’t really mesh well with today’s gaming culture. Bombrush Cyberfunk feels like it’s meant to be played with an audience, whether that’s chatting with friends or streaming. It’s not the kind of game that demands your full attention because, outside of the solid story, the gameplay is just mediocre. You’ve got three skills with three variants for BMX, skateboards, and skates, plus their powered-up versions. But honestly, it’s boring. It’s so terribly boring. There’s a lot to do, but none of it feels challenging, everything is repetitive, and exploration just doesn’t feel meaningful. Need a high score? Rail ride in circles, boost your gauge, do the same powered up skill, return to the rail. You've beaten the rival gang. Nice!

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
This game isn’t worth the asking price. It feels more like a $15 title, but the only real justification for the high price seems to be the licensed music. The gameplay elements, reminiscent of games like Tony Hawk and Jet Set Radio, haven’t aged well. Here, the mechanics are much more basic and toned back, with little to no customization unless you mod the game (which I’d definitely recommend if you play it).

So. Bomb Rush Cyberfunk. As someone who absolutely adored the original Jet Set Radio growing up, I was super pumped that this came out. And, I gotta say, it is absolutely a spiritual successor to that game.

For good and ill.

Going back to JSR after years away from it, it has jank. Hella jank. 1 analog stick on the dream cast controller, so only a trigger for camera recentering. Janky movement and acceleration, mildly irritating hitboxes and physics. In the modern age, it is not a good game. But it had something that Bomb Rush Cyberfunk doesn't, and that's failure states.

In JSR, each mission is a timed score attack mode. You have only a certain amount of time to get points, and combos and graffiti tagging are how you do it. More lines, better combos, more complex graffiti, more points. You're racing against the clock, and you can fail, drop your combo, or fuck up a graffiti spray and lose the points for that spot.It also had the problem that it was EXTREMELY linear. If you don't get the Jet rank in a mission, you have to wait till you hit that mission again in new game plus.

BRC got rid of that, at least... mostly by not having any real missions at all. The time attack portions, if you could even call them that, are few and far between, and you'll spend most of your time exploring the open world and mindlessly tagging spots. Even the spray painting, which is probably one of the more important parts, was dumbed down to "just mash at the wall". You get more multipliers if you graffiti new murals during a combo, but you're not actually doing anything skilful, and even if you don't do a new mural, you're not locked out, you can just try again at the next. You can't even fall while doing tricks. Sure, you'll lose your combo, but you can't die unless you fall into water, or get hurt by the cops.

Right, the cops. Eventually the cops will come out in greater force, and (so far what I've found) the only way to deescalate them/escape them is to wipe the stars entirely. Because the way that JSR did it, you have stakes as you try to eek out the last points before the cops kill you on a timer, escaping them. In BSR, you just reset them, because they got rid of the timed element. And then they immediately come back in, each successive mural giving you another star (with the small cutscene taking you out of the action to let you know that SHIELD GUYS ARE BACK for the fiftieth time).

It really feels like BRC is "open world JSR" but without the necessary gameplay changes and improvements needed to facilitate that change to a new style. So much taken out, nothing added back in. Time pressure removed. Graffiti skill checks removed. Level rankings removed. No differences in characters. Revamped spray can resourcing (nah, just kidding, removing it). 

So what does it add? 
- A boost system, which would be good if it let you keep your speed (it doesn't). after you finish a boost, you immediately brake back down to a standstill and have to reaccelerate in your normal movement style.
- A new combo multiplier system. This is potentially the one place that I want to 100% commend. Unlike Tony Hawk style games, where each new trick gives you combo multiplier, meaning you are incentivized to do the "infinite manual", BRC only gives you combo multiplier for new corners, wallrides and half pipes, meaning you're incentivized to make your combo go all around the play area. this is a great change.
-A terrrrrriiiiibbbblllllle cell phone camera.

BRC is great if you wanted JSR to open up and just be a place where you can skate around and listen to cool tunes and see cool art, but little else has changed in the last twenty years.

If I had any changes I'd want to make:
- More character differentiation. Even the movement styles (rollerblades, skate board and bmx) don't feel that different.
- Score/Time Attack
- Reasons to care about the murals you're painting
- Less "cutscenes" that stop the action. Don't need one for every heat level, don't need them for the tiny "crew member name" tag spots, potentially don't need them for the "hey kid, do this line" missions.
- Make the police something that you can't just deal with with a bathroom break.

I spent endless hours on JSR on Dreamcast. The game has not aged well due to very clunky controls and an awful graffiti mechanic. I was very hyped for this game because I thought that it could bring a new spin to the formula, but other than some slight changes to the mechanics, this game is just JSR3, which wouldn't be such a bad thing, except for the core game loop and the map design.

The game is boring, period. The maps are hard to parse and navigate, which makes finding satisfying lines more difficult than it should be. Many graffiti spots are very hidden and the game doesn't offer any guidance as to where they may be (it's possible to collect an item that will reveal all spots in an area but this item is also well hidden). And since the game loop revolves around finding enough spots to progress the story while avoiding enemies, it means that playing the game becomes a nuissance rather than a good time.

That's the game. Move around, paint enough graffiti and move to the next area, with some instances of battle jams in which you need to score as many points as possible. You can fight against enemies (sometimes you are required to) but the fighting system is just bad. I was honestly hoping for new ideas, but either Team Reptile didn't have any or they did not want to mess with the formula because they wanted to cater to nostalgics.

The tricking system, while welcome (I only played JSRF for like 30 minutes so I don't remember if it had it) it's also trivial and not fun. The graffiti system is vastly improved over JSR but other than allowing you to choose which graffiti to paint, the minigame doesn't really add that much and breaks the flow of the game (which is also a problem in the original JSR). Wallriding is incredibly confusing because you can only do it on certain surfaces which aren't clearly marked (other than signs). Upside-down rails are cool but they are not clearly marked either. The walk/ride switching animation is ridiculously slow. The phone UI is a pain in the ass to use, even more so when you're in the middle of a line or avoiding enemiea and you don't know whether the incoming message is actually useful or a stupid tip you already knew. The camera is not very smart and it makes calculating distances when jumping between rails much more difficult than it should.

The art direction is a nice throwback to JSR but sadly, the choices they made for the maps make the interactive elements hard to parse. The one thing that is unequivocally great is the soundtrack, which I love.

Overall, I'm disappointed. I wasn't expecting the best game ever, but after 20 years of videogame design progress and evolution, I hoped that this game would offer something new yet familiar. Instead, it offers an old and stale formula along with questionable map design. Or perhaps in my old age I just can't appreciate videogames anymore, since I play less and less every year.

While it may be the closest thing to a Jet Set Radio game in years and definitely better than all the other attempts on the market, this game still falls short. It certainly nailed the look of a JSR game, but not the feel. I think this is the result of two major issues. 

The first issue is just basic level design. Simply put, a lot of the stunts aren't lined up correctly. They're either too close, too far, or slightly off to the side which leads to an awkward clunky feel and many pointless falls. Jumps that would be very easy to gauge in a JSR game are over complicated here for no reason. JSR had a vast amount of control on how far you want to try and jump simply by easing up on movement or pushing full throttle following high momentum build up. Here, the movement is snappy and it will jerk the player forward exactly x ft, or snap the character to face 90 degrees in another direction.

Many of the areas in this game are just too wide, flat, and open. Everything feels super far apart, often times getting a collectible or graffiti involves going through a several minute gauntlet and requires you to fall off at the end and go all the way back through it again. This makes some levels very tedious and downright boring. Unlike JSR or JSRF where you can practically get through the entire game without touching the ground, this game just doesn't offer enough rails and routes through levels. A lot of rails simply lead to nothing and require you hold a button to slide across flat ground to continue your combo.

The other reason why I feel this game falls short of JSR games is where they decided to change things up to make it different. The territory battles are not fun or engaging what so ever. Granted, the JSR games had their issues with the racing and back tag graffiti but at least it felt like a game. In this game you just do more stunts to earn more points than the other gang. The issue is your arsenal of stunts is half of what was available in JSR. In order to get the most amount of points guaranteed is just to sit on a rail with turns in it, and lean into the turns for multipliers. This doesn't feel skillful, its repetitive, and you could practically do it with your eyes closed.

Then there's subtle design elements that are just annoying or pointless. Essentially being forced to change your character's color pallet to lose the police. The bathrooms in which you swap out your clothes are often difficult to spot, I don't want to change my colors, it instantly gets rid of the police, and you don't even need to lose the police cause any NPC conversation bypasses them chasing you. I really hate how each character in your gang has unique reputation scores in specific parts of the map depending on how much graffiti they did. Its unnecessary and seems like it can potentially soft lock you out of content if you spread rep across too many characters? Last time I checked, we were a crew not individual graffiti artists. I would also like to play as whoever I want but the game forces you to play as the main character Red for every story event. Its strongly suggesting you just play as him and no one else in this first playthrough.

To recap, while this is the closest thing to another JSR game compared to competitors, objectively its not as good. Usually with nostalgic titles you can take a vet's opinion with a mountain of salt, but this game is just clunky and weirdly designed around the edges. I also don't get whats going on around the forums, the devs wanted to capitalize off of JSR fans by making a spiritual successor but can't handle being labeled a clone or ripoff. For those JSR fans who are disappointed, do not lose hope. There are a lot of rumors on the street that the JSR games will be remastered or get a new game relatively soon.

Now before you pull out your pitchforks and torches.  It's not a bad game by any stretch,  but it lacks in a lot of areas compared to it's roots.  The gameplay loop is solid enough and it's fun.  In fact, it has improved over some aspects of the Jet Set franchise, like the boost mechanic, the tagging system, the multiple items you can use like skateboards and bikes.  It feels smooth and responsive compared to its predecessors.  


Bomb Rush Cyberfunk has a serviceable story, but it feels like it skirts around its themes rather than fully embracing them. In contrast, the Jet Set series is unapologetically rooted in its punk identity. You could argue that Jet Set’s story isn’t particularly strong, and its gameplay feels outdated by modern standards, but its levels, music, and overall aesthetic work together to convey its message loud and clear. It doesn’t just reference rebellion—it embodies it, making its themes feel more integral to the experience. 

BRCF’s music is kind of lackluster and not as diverse as I had hoped. Some tracks are okay, while others feel flat and uninteresting—so much so that I often turn it off and listen to my own collection instead.

I have to say, the Hideki Naganuma tracks sound phoned in and overly gamified. While I'm not trying say that game music isn’t real music or that Hideki Naganuma isn’t a great artist—he absolutely is. However, these particular tracks don’t stand well on their own, and he’s certainly made better work in the past.

It’s not music I’d want to blast in my car; it’s more suited for background listening while working on a project. The Jet Set Radio series soundtracks, on the other hand, are far more diverse and hold up well on their own—featuring punk, garage rock, house, drum and bass, hip-hop, hard rock, and more

  
In conclusion, Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is a very solid game that successfully captures the spirit of classic skating and graffiti titles with its vibrant aesthetic, energetic soundtrack, and fluid movement. However, while it excels in style and nostalgia, it falls short in certain areas of execution, such as level design, mission variety, or depth of mechanics. Despite these flaws, it remains an enjoyable experience for fans of the genre and those looking for a stylish, fast-paced urban adventure

This is a difficult game to review negatively, cause I love what it's going for and enjoy pretty much everything about it, *except* playing it. I'll try to cover my points as best I can.

The primary issue is simply the fact it's so repetitive. It's not that short of a game, it's about 10 to 12 hours, maybe more if you want a full 100%. Yet by the 3 hour mark you have seen pretty much everything it has to offer. There are 3 different "gear" types, skateboard, rollerblades, and bikes, but they all control exactly the same. And you'll be doing all the same stuff in every area you explore throughout the story. It's so boring in fact I can't get myself to finish it.

Alongside this the trick system feels completely superfluous. You get multipliers just by grinding on rails, and have exactly 3 tricks for every gear type. You press the button and it plays a canned animation, and it just feels very disconnected and floaty. They all chain into each other seamlessly but not really in a way that feels all-that cool because you only have THREE tricks! You also have a move that lets you keep your combo going quite generously even if you hit the floor, so there is virtually no challenge at all for any score attack sections of the game, and getting a high combo or score feels completely unrewarding because it's so absurdly easy to do. I'm so surprised that there is zero depth to this, like no combo tricks, or just, literally fricking anything to give it spice lol. The trick system feels like a prototype, it does not feel finished.

On an extra note about difficulty, the police system is completely pointless and provides zero threat. Which is a polar opposite to Jet Set Radio, feels like they really missed the mark there.

The story itself I did find interesting, the presentation is great and it has a fun mystery element. The visuals are also just gorgeous and the dream sequences especially are very fun. I actually enjoyed the linear sequences of platforming the most in this game because it feels like the only time it's trying to challenge you. And they are well designed challenges.

The music selection is *mostly* good but quite frankly some songs are obnoxious. "Hair Dun Nails Dun" might be the worst piece of music I have heard in my entire life and I absolutely hate it lol.

But yeah, it's an experience that feels overall very shallow. There is zero challenge besides the rare linear platforming sequence. The movement on its own feels nice, but doesn't really give you much room for player expression because the trick system is depressingly simple. And again, the other 2 gear types have no differences to them either. This does capture the *vibe* it's aiming for very well, but it needed more depth to really feel like it could stand on its own. As it is now, it just feels like an undercooked JSR fangame.

I don't condone any illegal activity. But if, hypothetically speaking, there was a way to emulate old consoles and you could play / replay JSRF. You should just do that and have a much better time.
