Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is everything you want in a Jet Radio spiritual successor: dripping with style, an interesting world, smooth controls, and an eargasmic soundtrack. Yes, everything you'd want... except a satisfying gameplay loop.

The problem isn't that that Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is not an arcadey, race the clock, high-scoring graffiti-em-up; it'd be fine if it kept the stylish trappings of its inspiration but went a different way with the core mechanics and challenge. It feels like the game left out the game entirely.

Most charitably, Bomb Rush Cyberfunk's core game is a 3D Platformer Collectathon, but instead of collecting Power Moons or Jiggies the game is figuring out how to reach the tagging spots scattered throughout the level, as well as the occasional music track, costume, or graffiti style. It also throws in the occasional "trick combo scoring" challenge and boss fight to mix it up, but neither of those are particularly interesting, for reasons I'll explain. It's all just a bit... boring.

Tricks and Combos and Scoring: This is the closest the game gets to a clever mechanic - you rack up combo multiplier by stringing elements together (specifically: wall runs, ramps, and sharp corners), with each unique element only counting once. If you're not on an element, you have a limited time to manual to a new one or the combo ends, encouraging you to scout the stage for a line that combos as much new stuff as possible. 

Unfortunately, the game faceplants this mechanic in two ways. First, it quickly teaches a mechanic that lets you manual infinitely, eliminating the challenge of finding a tight line through the stage. Second, there's no downside to repeating an element, just no new multiplier. In almost every challenge, it's enough to hit a 10x-20x multiplier from rail corners and then just grind a single loop forever while mashing buttons so you don't risk losing combo. It would have been much stronger if the game focused on stringing as many elements (including graffitti spots, which are hardly rewarded!) in a combo without repeat, as the stages are clearly designed for lines like that!

Combat: Boost into things and kick them. If it's a machine, kick it and graffiti it. There's a fun mechanic where you can tag a cop the moment you deal the killing blow to it, but the window is very small and there's no reward for doing it. If the game forced you to tag police to defeat them it would have been unique and interesting, but here it's just a silly nod.

Besides, outside of the four or so (very short) boss fights, the police element is pointless. In the Jet Radio games, the police presence got worse as the stage wore on, and they could interrupt your tags, requiring you to frantically put enough distance between you and them to get your tag in before they could catch you, then book it under the gun of the clock. In Bomb Rush Cyberfunk, there's no stage timer and no risk of cops interrupting your work, making them just kind of annoying when they spawn. And the mechanic is rendered entirely pointless by the fact that you can clear all police presence by touching a bathroom, so the mechanic might as well not have been included at all during free stage exploration.

Characters: In the Jet Radio games, different characters had different stats like health and graffiti combo length that affected scoring and strategy. In Bomb Rush Cyberfunk, they all... look different. It feels like a mechanic introduced just because the Jet Radio games had them, and not because it adds anything.

In conclusion, Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is an homage to everything you remember about the Jet Radio games, minus the _game_. While I did enjoy my time with it just for the style alone, I honestly can't recommend it to anyone - there's not enough interesting gameplay here to attract anyone not familiar with its inspiration, and for fans of the inspiration the game feels like a shell of what it's inspired by. If I could give it a thumbs-middle, I might, but not at $40.

Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is a game that draws too much inspiration from its 1 source and fails to do anything to call its own.

It's been 23 years since Jet Set Radio came out, you really couldn't create anything unique to your own game? The music and visuals absolutely kick ass, but, once you're done appreciating those BRC doesn't do anything to really hook the players in.

Game-play as stated earlier is very bare-bones and unimaginative. Each form of mobility is mechanically the same, save for the bicycle which grants you access to 2 new areas as part of the story. The combat as necessitated from part of the story handles very poorly and seriously misses out on the opportunity to involve the players transportation option as a usable combat tool. You got 3 buttons for performing tricks & combat moves but there's no skill ceiling for how they function or really any way to get better at the game. Pulling a manual is done at the press of a button and absolutely cheapens the game's score system basically allowing you to infinitely keep up a combo so long as you have a brain. The additional player characters are all reskins but they're locked to their respective modes of transport.

On the topic of performing tricks, they're all incredibly absolutely underwhelming. There's little to no impact on actually performing anything. Sound effects are so quiet or even just tame and the visuals don't really do much to emphasize anything. The experience of handling the game from minute 1 to hour 10 is exactly the same. The game-play loop no different. Go to area, spray paint, fight whoever, go to the next area. The actual gang battles I was excited for because it actually lent some use to the scoring system but every gang fight is incredibly easy with absolutely little to no challenge whatsoever.

I'm unable to walk away from this game understanding why it has so much praise or what all the hype's about, there's absolutely no argument to be had when I say that skating games of yesteryear are far more mechanically involved and actually fun to play. When I look at this, I see a tool for modding and really nothing else. It's a shame that this game blows so hard.

The work that Team Reptile put together for Lethal League Blaze absolutely blows this game out of the water by miles and it's genuinely disappointing that what we have of BRC is the product of all the years spent in development.

[b]Introduction[/b]

I went into Bomb Rush Cyberfunk with pretty high hopes. I really enjoyed Jet Set Radio when I played it a few years ago and 100% it on Steam, and seeing this so highly praised as a spiritual successor, I was very excited to try it out. But after just completing the game and getting all of the achievements, I don't really understand the massive positive reception it has received at all. For most of my playtime it was exceedingly boring and notably worse than Jet Set Radio in almost every single way. It is a different 'style' of game and I've heard it more closely compared to the sequel, Jet Set Radio Future, so maybe I went in with the wrong expectations, but I nonetheless do not get the appeal.

[b]Gameplay[/b]

Bomb Rush Cyberfunk's core gameplay loop is very, very boring. Basically, you go to a new area, tag some spots with graffiti to earn enough rep to lure out the rival gang and then challenge them to a style battle. It's not too dissimilar to Jet Set Radio, but the most notable difference is the lack of pressure or difficulty of any kind. The police don't show up until you're halfway done and are extremely easy to avoid. They're no threat at all. At best, the turrets that slow you down are kind of annoying, the rest of the enemy types are so non-threatening that I didn't even realise they were there a lot of the time. If it does get too much at the higher heat levels, you can just go into a portable toilet and immediately clear all your heat and any cop presence. You can only use them once, but they can be refreshed simply by exiting and reentering a level and there are multiple per level.

For some reason, the developers also thought that what Jet Set Radio needed was shovelware beat em up combat that feels very janky and floaty and just awful in general to perform in any capacity. And you can't just not engage with it because the game forces you to engage in it at multiple points throughout the story including for several very poor boss fights. I have no idea what the appeal of the combat is supposed to be or why the developers decided to include it.

The lack of pressure and difficulty wouldn't be as much of an issue if the levels were interesting to traverse, but they're not really at all, with the exception of Pyramid Island in the game's fourth chapter. They're very large, empty and boring with often only one linear route to the bulk of the tagging spots despite its openness. Pyramid Island breaks this convention a little with its focus on upwards navigation using multiple grind rail routes and is by far the best level, but it's the [i]bare minimum[/i] of what I was expecting in terms of level design going into this game, yet it's the game's peak and is notably worse both before and after.

The game's trick system is also very uninteresting and has 0 depth. You can perform a total of three tricks while grinding and three more variations when boosting which are all mapped to three buttons. You can win every trick battle by leaning into a few corners while grinding which increases your multiplier and then doing a few tricks while boosting which massively increases your base score. That's about it. There's no worry you'll drop your combo because you can hold right trigger to manual automatically when you hit the ground and can maintain it for roughly ten seconds or even longer if you have boost or forever if there's a slope. There are three types of vehicle: skateboard, rollerskates and bike. But they have no functional differences and are just a cosmetic change except for 3, maybe 4 occasions where you arbitrarily need a bike or skateboard to open up a path.

Credit where credit is due, the Super Mario Sunshine platforming levels at the end of each chapter are pretty creative and consistently fun to go through. But unfortunately they amount to only about 5% of the game at most. The final boss was also surprisingly good, mainly because it didn't use the game's shitty combat system like most of the rest.

[b]Graphics[/b]

The graphics are good and replicate Jet Set Radio's style fairly well, but feels a lot more subdued in its colour palette, and the character designs are a massive step down from Jet Set Radio's characters. There are some good character designs, notably Red, Tryce, DJ Cyber and the Oldheads are those I'd consider to be the best. But others are genuinely horrendously bad. The rival gangs in the second half of the game are very boring and bland, the extra characters you can unlock like Mesh look like generic NPCs and the flat colours on Bel and Vinyl's outfits and their painted on eyes look awful. Yes, it's trying to recreate the Dreamcast's technically limited graphics, but none of the characters in Jet Set Radio look anywhere near as bad as its worst and are much more visually expressive and unique across the board. Compare Bel to Gum or Vinyl to Pirahna. Look up Mew or Cube or Slate or Combo and you'll immediately see the massive difference in quality.

[b]Music[/b]

I may be in the minority here, but I found the soundtrack to be the game's most disappointing aspect. Hideki Naganuma's tracks are predictably excellent and contain plenty of that signature Jet Set Radio funk, but the rest of the soundtrack leaves a lot to be desired. I hesitate to call the rest of the music 'bad' but it is largely repetitive and tedious to listen to as well as being far from funky. Most of the music falls into pop or hip hop and is generally very mellow and low key. You could definitely argue that this is Bomb Rush Cyberfunk going for its own identity rather than copying Jet Set Radio wholesale and this kind of music fits better with the more relaxed gameplay, but it holds little appeal for me. Songs like AGUA were driving me insane with their repetitiveness and as soon as I got the Locking Up the Funk mixtape, which contains Hideki's tracks as well as two of the best non-Hideki tracks, I listened to that on loop for the rest of my playthrough because I honestly couldn't stomach most of the other tracks. Very few tracks even come close to hitting the same as "Let Mom Sleep" or "Sneakman" or "Rock It On" or 90% of Jet Set Radio's OST.

[b]Story[/b]

The story is about the only area where I think Bomb Rush Cyberfunk improves over its progenitor. The characters are pretty bland personality wise, but the central mystery around the protagonist is executed fairly well and ends with a surprising twist that leads to a pretty satisfying conclusion with one of the game's most kickass moments. I don't think a good story is important or even necessary at all for this kind of game, but it's nonetheless worthy of some praise.

[b]Other Minor Issues I Have[/b]

-Like the different vehicles, characters have no stat changes like Jet Set Radio and play functionally exactly the same.

-You're invincible while spraying graffiti and the minigame is impossible to fail, making the police even less of a threat.

-Spraying medium and large graffiti plays a short animation that locks your movement, which is fine, but it's the same for small graffiti which is often on billboards or in a row next to railings. The animation interrupts the movement flow and gets a little annoying. Jet Set Radio solved this problem two decades ago by not playing an animation cutscene for small graffiti.

[b]Conclusion[/b]

Overall, Bomb Rush Cyberfunk looks like Jet Set Radio and sounds like Jet Set Radio if you don't listen too closely, but ultimately lacks its soul and spirit. Even if you do like this style of game compared to Jet Set Radio, I cannot recommend it for its current price. I'd hesitate to recommend it for even [i]half[/i] its current price. I'm glad I got it for cheap in a Humble Bundle along with several other games for cheap so it tempered some of my disappointment and I'd recommend other people do the same or wait for a 70+% discount at the least.

As a huge fan of JSR(F) I really wanted to like this game. I wasn't expecting a carbon copy, but I was at least expecting a game released 20+ years later to be better. 

The controls are clunky, the combo system is lackluster, the soundtrack is overall a solid 3/10, and the writing for the story is really cheesy and full of tropes/weird plot devices. The turbo boosting system is really boring and slow. For as large as the bar can be charged it is depleted quickly, but takes so much effort to rebuild. The speed gained from boosting is mid. Boosting on rails seems to gain 0 speed. 

Whoever designed the menu and the maps did a fantastic job, but nearly all mechanics within the gameplay department unrefined. This should realistically cost 15 USD. I have no idea how a 40 USD price tag is justifiable to anyone. I beat the game in 9 hours and was trying to take it slow. 40 USD for 9 hours is simply not worth it. The flow of gameplay also appear to have been intentionally spread out thin to pad game hours. While the maps are large, they are barren and uneventful. There are also so many cut scenes that interrupt the flow of the game. It's like eating a salad but they replaced croutons with rocks. The cut scenes are usually jarring and time wasting, too. 

The core gameplay is repetitive. linear, predictable, and tedious. Every map plays the same. Tag up designated spots, build up rep, challenge the enemy gang members to individual swag-off competitions, unlock a section the old heads are bogarding to earn additional rep, challenge the whole enemy team to an effortless score competition, and then finally have fun on the flashback maps just to move on to a new burough to do the exact same thing. 

After finishing the game and monitoring my FPS throughout my entire time playing, it is safe to say the optimization is horrendous. With an eVGA 3090 FTW3 and a Ryzen 7 5800X and 32GB of RAM, I should not be getting 75-90 FPS in a game with this sort of graphical fidelity. I get similar FPS in battlefield 2042, which has tremendously more detail. This is inexcusable. 

Additionally, the developers seemingly have not continued to update the game with new content and QoL fixes after making their money. Instead, they released 25 USD worth of DLC for an already egregiously priced game.

This game was fun, but not worth $40.

I enjoyed the game but I don't think it's worth $40. I also think the percentage of positive reviews misrepresents the quality of the game so I'm giving this game a thumbs down to help offset that. It has been clearly established by other reviews and coverage of the game that this is a spiritual successor to Jet Set Radio. I never played those games before and therefore had no nostalgia for them going into Bomb Rush Cyberfunk. 

Let me start with what I enjoyed. The aesthetic and overall vibe of this game is fantastic. From the colorful cell shaded graphics to the music to the campy dialogue, it all comes together to create a fun world that you want to lose yourself in. The trick system is also a lot of fun. It's surprisingly basic for a skating game but it works and trying to go for a new high combo score in each area is a lot of fun. 

Now onto the negatives...

1) Most of my playtime during the main story quest was trying to figure out where to go next. Many times you need to find a certain NPC or hit a certain number of graffiti spots in an area but the game either never tells you where they are or how to get to them. Some people might enjoy wandering around trying to find a solution to these objectives but I just found it tedious after a point. 

2) Main story is very short. If you know what you are doing you can probably complete it in under 5 hours easy. 

3) Game is in dire need of more music tracks. Each story chapter features 3-4 music tracks that just loop over and over. This got annoying when I was spending over an hour per chapter. thanks to point #1. 

4) Game is not fully voice acted. Instead characters will just repeat the same couple words and phrases. JSR was fully voice acted and I feel like the developers should look into updating this game with full voice acting since the cutscenes feel rather flat without it. 

5) Cutscenes feature very stiff and basic animations most of the time. Hi-Fi rush features much smoother cutscene animations and that game is $30 while this game is somehow $40...

6) Level design gets progressively worse as the game goes on. The early levels/areas are more open and feature many branching pathways. The manner in which you can explore them feels a lot more free. Later areas have a much more linear structure where there is only a single path that can be taken to get to other major sections. I would say level design takes a nosedive at around chapter 3 or 4. They look good aesthetically but the layout does not gel with the gameplay and overall vibe the game is going for. 

7) The finale is super rushed. The final boss fight just kind of happens without much buildup and the fight itself is rather underwhelming which leads me to my next point.

8) This game has combat and it is super basic. You have 3 different melee attack buttons that all essentially do the same thing and you can use your spray-paint. You essentially just mindlessly mash the melee attack buttons and maybe use your spray-paint to get rid of human troops. The mechs require you to graffiti them in a certain spot to destroy them. Overall combat feels clunky and I think they should have added more depth to it.

9) I'm sure many will disagree with me on this but I would prefer for the game to show me where all the graffiti spots and collectables are on the minimap from the start. I know you can see all the graffiti spots when you find the map but I don't think finding the map should be a requirement for this. It would make the game much more pleasant since players will spend less time wandering around aimlessly trying to find maps, graffiti spots, and collectibles.

10) Why does the main story feature multiple instances of [spoiler]decapitation and body transplants[/spoiler]? It's kinda gross and doesn't really fit the overall aesthetic and vibe of the game imo. Most people probably won't care about this and I wouldn't either if this game was a different genre but it doesn't really work for me here...

Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is a handheld (Nintendo Switch)/console game that's also been put on Steam as a bit of an afterthought, as it's very much designed for the handheld/console gaming audience.

It's a thematic ripoff of another, much older "street funk" console game called Jet Set Radio, designed of course for console peasants, much as this is.  The idea is that you are a funky cool street dancer who is arrested and you have to skateboard, dance and fight in weak and cringey street dance battles while godawfully bad music plays.  

On the upside, the game does feature customisable controls and resolution, so at least some of the basic, minimum requirements have been met.  Unfortunately there's a number of other technical defects and shortcomings which contribute to the game being difficult to recommend to gamers.

The game features low-polygon "retro" assets with a cel-shading type shader effects instead of doing their job properly and texturing the game assets, making this look like a barely functional 3D game from the early 1990s.  This visual style is a method that lazy devs often use when they have a lack of interest/capability to create highly detailed, high poly models and instead use shader effects to disguise that shortcoming under the name of "art", or "We made it look bad on purpose", which really isn't something gamers should have to put up with.  It's unclear why the developers weren't willing to arrange high quality, high polygon count contemporary assets and high resolution textures for the game.  It's far below the state of the art visuals gamers expect as a result of their decisions.

Instead of bothering to hire voice actors (and they certainly priced this game as if they had), it's just the occasional grunt and "huh" and "yeah" during the console game cutscenes that you're bombarded with as you click through lines of pointless dialog... yes, once more console developers failed to understand the crucial gaming axiom, "Show, don't tell". 

Another defect in the game caused by the console-peasant-centric design is the intolerably bad camera controls, as you'll often run into situations where the camera flips around or you just don't get a good view of the action.  Console peasants are used to this, PC gamers are used to having more accurate and fine control over games.  Whether the developers decided not to fix this defect when porting the game, or they just don't care because they never played PC games before is irrelevant.

This defect springs from the limitations of inferior console peasant children's toy gamepads, but on PC we don't have this limitation due to KB+M controls... however, the developer deliberately chose to arrogantly foist this handicap onto PC gamers.  Out of spite, or laziness, it's unclear, regardless, once more console peasants and console devs have made gaming worse for everyone.

Because this is designed for handheld/portable gaming appliances, it carries a number of other deliberate design deficiencies and shortcomings.  Compromises were made to cater to the low power handheld gaming appliances that the game was designed for.  These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the mobile game developers.  The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for low power handhelds forces upon a game.  While this might run well on a Steam Deck, we must remember the vast majority of gamers here are gaming on PC.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

In an attempt to excuse the low quality of delivery here, the game makes a big point of having a nice soundtrack.  If the business plan for a game is to compete with Spotify, which is free and has effectively unlimited music, all of which is better than the music here, it's failed before it even started. Gamers can listen to the Spotify for free.  A game cannot be seen as recommendable just because it competes badly with listening to the radio or to MP3s.

So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 110,000+ games on Steam?

Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is so incredibly far from being AAA, but it delusionally carries the full AAA price of $40 USD, for which you could easily get any number of actual AAA games designed for PC.

Unfortunately Steam reviewers aren't presented with a "Maybe" option... if they did, that's what I'd choose.  This isn't a completely bad game, but it's also not one of the best.  As always, if you read my review and you can overlook the negatives I've called out, or they just aren't important to you, then by all means go ahead and buy this, but I think you can probably do better.

BRC is probably one of the most disappointing games I've ever played in my life. This is one of my favorite studios, doing a spiritual sequel to one of my favorite IPs of all time, and yet somehow they dropped the ball in several major ways that make me no longer want to play this game after finishing my single playthru.

Firstly, the music, art, and vibe are all solid--this does feel like a proper JSRF sequel in that regard at least. The new graffiti system is fun to use, and the movement in general also feels very solid.

It's just after playing for a few hours that you realize what we have here is barely an update to the old Jet Set formula, with almost no quality of life changes of any kind to make the experience of playing the game actually more fun.

Firstly, tricks are boring--there are no actual specific inputs that mean anything, so to 'trick' all you're doing is mashing buttons. This is kind of fun at first, but it feels incredibly rote and monotonous after just a little bit of playtime, and I have no idea why the system wasn't expanded more.

The story is delivered in non-voiced cutscenes, which makes no sense to me considering the DJ voice-overs in JSRF were one of the best piece of the entire package. The story itself is borderline nonsensical, complete with a last second info-dump plot twist that made me basically hate the entire narrative I'd been forced to go through. Not having the character's properly voiced but still using VA work for incidentals makes absolutely no sense to me, and it seems either like a poor stylistic choice or a budget constraint.

The last and biggest issue with this game is that the act of skating around, collecting stuff, is not fun. Collectibles are only sometimes marked on your map, which means more than often you'll be stumbling around blindly hoping that you see something shiny in the distance, and then not to lose track of it again. All you had to do was add indicators to the mini-map for collectibles and it would basically fix the entire game, but they didn't, and there isn't even a mod for it.

The achievements at the end-level for this game are incredibly monotonous, grindy, and boring. I cannot believe this is what we got after all these years of waiting for a spiritual sequel to such a great series.

I'm still going to recommend this game since it was decently fun for a few hours and there hasn't been anything else like it in a long time, but if you're like me and you were hoping this game would blow your socks off, you'll probably be severely disappointed. Somehow everyone else seems to love it, but this barely feels like an upgrade to JSRF, and in some places (like level design and VA) it is actively worse. The last few levels you access in this game have stupid height-based chokepoint navigation that means accessing half the stage is impossible unless you take a very specific path, which means no fluid transitions between height levels or areas, just following the dumb linear path until you access the next circular tricking area.

Actually I changed my mind, I'm not recommending this game. It sucks.

Secondly, there is no energy to this game. Remember how the original Jet Set Radio opens up? With Professor K’s iconic JET SET RADDIOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO blaring into your eardrums. That game commanded your attention from the start and you, the player, knew you were in for a ride. Here, there’s no voice acting. Sure, we get some grunts and a few short words here and there from the many characters, but you can’t help but notice that something is missing from the cutscenes. The trick system is very shallow, very easy to maintain and get a ridiculously high score. Once you understand the systems, it's honestly just yourself sabotaging yourself if you manage to lose a good chain, or you hit a set of stairs (Which auto-force you off your skates regardless if you land on the flat part or the actual stairs themselves.) Once you get the combo system down, all the challenge of movement goes out the window. 

But part of the problem comes from the lack of clarity of various mechanics. There's a lot of people that don't know you can use Inline Skates to break glass by gliding on it beneath you, or that you can use a skateboard on firehydrants to get extra air. That bicycles open unique garages, or that running has a singular attack (Carthweel) that chains into a super-jump for getting over / on top of obstacles. The complete lack of clarity and ambiguity the game left in these regards means you might be frustrated until you find the answer yourself through sheer luck, or by looking up an answer to it online.

The game feels like it really missed out from genuine QoL testing and a lack of understanding. Everytime you're bombing an area, you'll be constantly forced to re-watch the same introduction cutscene. The minimap is abysmal at best, not marking anything of import on it even once you obtain the map. Bathroom stalls are used to change your outfit as well as to dump infamy to get the police off you. Cipher gatherings are supposed to change characters and Taxi locations don't auto-unlock based on area; meaning you likely won't unlock the Taxi's until you want to use one in the post-game, only to find that you haven't unlocked any because the usual expectation that the fast travel system would be a baseline unlock actually requires you to do so individually (And also to find them.) 

But nothing important is put on the map itself, aside from tag spots, once you unlock the map. There's no effective way of tracking your collectibles you've gathered. There's constant glitches on points for bombing each area. 

Not only that, the story really only focuses on a small group. There's a few obscure optional characters but unlike JSRF, you never really feel like they're 'part of the process' of playing, rather they feel like out-of-the-way optional sidequests with trivially easy objectives to complete. The graffiti and authoritarian police force in "Jet Set Radio" was a statement on freedom of expression. "Graffiti is art" (but vandalism is a crime, etc.). I am the target demographic for this game, having played both Jet Grind Radio & JSRF. I loved those games growing up and affectionately call this game nostalgia-bait. I followed their social media posts when I saw them and was generally excited for the game, even buying it on day 1 to show my support for games like these.

But I have been pretty disappointed by BRC and want to walk through why that is.

The Police
When I was grooving to the sweet tunes of BRC and ended up beating up a cop on a whim, it was never an interesting fight or a huge challenge, but these games are not combat-oriented so that is totally fine. What is not fine is how it felt like whenever I'd beat on a cop in my way, a short cutscene would play and more cops with higher stakes weapons would appear. So they are essentially telling me to either leave or hurry up with whatever my goal in the area is. What this incentivizes you to do as a player is to not engage with the police, which while thematic, feels awful the times you forget and try to use the game systems to mess around and do what feels natural and cool. Telling the players to not interact with the game world feels like a negative play pattern and I can't imagine why it was implemented how it is because it takes away from the awesome movement and tagging systems in place.

The Length
I don't want this review to focus on game length too much, but beating the game in 8 hours was definitely deflating. I actually enjoyed the narrative that was told - it wasn't some masterpiece but it was fun and over the top in ways I wanted to see in a game like this. And while I don't regret my purchase (more on that later) I would want more content in the tin for non-completionists like myself. Essentially I wanted to be in this world longer and see more twists and turns of the story as an excuse to stick around, but the core gameplay couldn't substitute for that.

The Levels
Almost everytime I loaded in a new area I was immediately taken in by how cool they all looked. The mall? Pyramid island? But the issues slowly seeped in, and are much more noticeable in the less inspired areas. These places are large, which is sweet, but they feel much more empty than they should be. The island is a good example, where all the sweet wild grinding areas make you hype to get around but getting to those parts means playing around in a less than interesting and very spread out area that has few real places of interest and does not feel lived in or fun to explore. Time and time again I would try to find my way up to a certain spot, end up missing a step or two and land back at the bottom. Once or twice I didn't mind but getting back up in certain areas just started to feel like a punishment, and often those sweet areas weren't even that great once i got there. Also some levels, like the bus station, felt a little too close to JSRF/Jet Grind Radio levels.

The Challenge
First I want to recognize that Team Reptile had a tough ask in front of them. I recall one or two parts of JSRF being oddly difficult, but the rest of the game being pretty reasonably easy/chill. Saying that, I still felt the game needed something more as the crew battles felt pretty formulaic by the endpoint. To their credit, I don't know of an ideal way to approach this end of things and frankly it might be the least of my critiques listed here. Combos are laughbly easy to chain and pull off, and while it was fun to do on my own for funsies it slowly got less and less exciting as it hard to be inventive with the limited moveset and all I had to do was find optimal parts of each level for multipliers, which was not an exciting thing to keep in the back of my head.

The Mechanics
Almost 80% of my way through the game I got a text from another character and they explained a new mechanic (about holding right trigger as I jump off of a grind). I have no idea why the game decided to wait this long to let me in on that, but it definitely made me hopeful I was at most 50% through the game. I don't love tutorialized mechanics but some more of that probably wouldn't have hurt.

Okay, those are my big gripes. It's a lot, I know, but now I can get to the rest of this review. The things I liked!

The Music
Holy wowza, the music in this game was fantastic. I just want it on shuffle and then it might be perfect.

The Style
They nailed everything I cared about visually too. These characters looked so good, and yes this is nostalgia speaking, but I loved all of it. The other gangs were awesome, which is perfect because I loved all the wild gangs in the other games. More wacky gangs please. The graffiti looks amazing, really sweet stuff and lots of amazing pieces to collect and tag.

Tagging
I am a little more torn on this one, but I think I really liked their tagging mechanics. The pausing while grinding felt a little jarring depending on context, but overall I love not worrying about spray cans as a resource. When I was able to tag things super fast were some of my most satisfying moments.

The Phone
This was a wonderful in-universe way of grounding us to a certain moment in time and to give real information to the players.

Conclusion
Earlier I mentioned I didn't regret this purchase, but as you can see I do not recommend this game. I really want Team Reptile to either add more content to this game, or I want them to make a sequel and work out the kinks that a new product like BRC is bound to have. Supporting them is a huge part of allowing companies to take risks like this, so while I wish the game was twice as long I want them to have my money so they can keep on keeping on. So much of the fundamentals are within reach and with BRC as a baseline I am hopeful they see the excitement and buzz a game like this has created and that the fanbase is hungry for more. I was so ready to fall in love with this game, but being honest I can't be so blinded by nostalgia when so many issues are so flagrantly present.

What little time I got to enjoy BRC was mostly a good time, but there wasn't nearly enough of it. I really want Team Reptile to take the lessons learned from this release and up the ante whenever they decide to revisit the world of New Amsterdam. I'll be more hesitant after these missteps, but I am hopeful they can course correct given time and love.

I am disappointed.

The style is good. The music is tight. The graffiti is cool. The tricks are neat. The movement is smooth.

But there is absolutely zero challenge, zero stakes, zero tension.

ALL of the characters are flatter than cardboard and ALL the cutscenes are boring, slow-paced, and lacking interesting angles. There are no characters that get me hyped like DJ Professor K did, and no character or mechanic to really make you feel like you're a part of the game world like DJ Professor K did. All of the unlockable characters aside from story ones have a few lines of dialogue and then just chill at your place forever. There isn't even any unique selection dialogue or special tricks only they can do, they are just glorified skins.

The cops are sterile and useless, yet are always presented as this incredible insurmountable force in all the cutscenes. The snipers are pitiful and going in a straight line is enough to throw them off. Instantly defeating any cop with a midair spray makes them incredibly easy to kill in batches. The bosses are incredibly easy to dodge and damage (and the normal cops are too of course). Health refills quickly and makes any mistakes overtly easy to correct. Everything feels completely unearned with the lack of stakes and ruins whatever tension could have been introduced with some of the cooler setpieces.

All 3 of the movement styles (board, skates, bike) handle [i]exactly the same[/i] with the only minute differences being 1) what special secret areas you can arbitrarily trigger and 2) the speed/duration of manuals, plus extra manual tricks you can do on the board. You can't ride backwards on skates (JSR staple) or bikes, and you can't ride goofy on boards. You always land perfectly and straight on regardless of what your state is midair; even JSR had the courtesy to spin you around if you would have landed weird. I get it's a style to have the game flow like this, but with such a focus on tricking, making it inconsequential to spam tricks is just pitiful. In fact, so much as touching a surface that so much as resembles stairs forces you into walking state and kills your combo—this is actually the only failure state I think the game has when it comes to the trick system, and even then it's a mere slap on the wrist. Actually being on foot at all is an inherent disadvantage and there is no reason for it to even be implemented. They axed the Soap shoes grind despite the animation still being in the game and I am pissed; no shoes grind makes on foot even more useless.

The 3 trick buttons are completely interchangable between eachother and on all movement styles, with the exact same durations and functionality; just spam all 3 buttons in linear sequence and you always get max points, it's brainless. If you dont care about getting max points (they are are plentiful and piss easy to acquire) then just spam one or two instead. Boost tricks are broken and can be used to effortlessly continue any combo forever, or gain max speed in exchange for a small and easily recouped piece of meter in the very same combo + meter gain multiplier you just extended.

Spraypainting is a fucking pain in the ass and was only cool the first time. It is actually possible to fail the spray minigame if you wait around for like 30 seconds but you can immediately start it again and get no penalty. The only incentive to spraying anything specific is achievements or personal taste. Once again, no failure states: just wiggle stick in a circle a few times so the annoying gameplay stoppage goes away.

The entire game is over-tutorialized and hand-holdy despite the fact they never tell you you can break into the secret areas or spray cops in the air, arguably two of the most useful abilities in the game (well the first isn't if you don't care about secrets). The game never tells you about the grounded trick jump but it's actually required to get a specific spray for completionism sake. Even if you dance on a Cyber pad (god what a fucking stupid name) before your idiotic mary sue of a gang partner tells you you can Cyber, nothing happens and you have to wait for his dumb ass to patronizingly tell you about them.

Many of the locales (and characters) are ripped from JSR[F] 1:1 in terms of aesthetics and prominent design. For example, the bus station and the hideout look like they could have been beta stages for JSR. Most of the grinds flow well but the fast speeds you can reach occasionally makes it difficult to continue combos with the props given, and there's rarely incentive to go max speed. 

I could keep fucking going but I'll probably hit the character limit.

Suffice to say: Game's fun if you turn your brain off, but severely lacking and I am very disappointed. If you want to relive JSR this'll do it, but it does little new and doesn't really push boundaries with what it does do. Honestly just go play JSRF.

BRC copies style, mechanics, and levels from the JSR and JSRF, but somehow makes them worse. Levels are now bigger, but they're also bland and empty. A lot of space is being wasted, and there isn't a good flow to them. 
The main goal is to tag graffiti, but there is a lot of filler in between. You need to go from point A to point B to meet a guy, who will tell you to meet another guy. Rinse and repeat. 

The tagging system is similar to JSR with a small minigame. However, in JSR, there wasn't any animation when you tag small graffiti, but there is in BRC, which ruins the flow and momentum.

BRC came out 20 years after the JSRF, but I would argue that JSRF looks better visually. They copied the cell shaded of JSRF, but everything looks empty and dead. There are hardly any pedestrians or NPCs walking around the streets, while JSRF featured large crowds of people on the original Xbox. JSRF also had better VFX, for example, when you use boost.
The controls are better than JSR but pretty much the same as JSRF. Maybe a touch less floaty.

Music is subjective, and some of the tracks in BRC are good and fit the overall vibe. However, there's a weird choice to have the same tracks play over and over again while you're in the same area. After a while, it became grating and I had to turn off the music. 

I don't put JSR or JSRF on a pedestal. I know those games were flawed even at release. JSR controls were super janky and floaty; there was a bunch of filler and badly designed levels, like the sewers. JSRF dropped all the challenging aspects of the game. Despite all of that, those games were cool and unique. BRC is not cool or unique; it's a copy of the older games. That would be fine because there hasn't been a sequel to JSRF, and there are no other games like it, but I feel like we deserved better.

This is one of those times I really wish Steam had a "mixed" review option. The good stuff is genuinely really good, but a recommendation doesn't feel right considering the problems and the current price ($40, or $20 on sale).

Good stuff: 

+ Visuals/Aesthetic
+ Soundtrack
+ Skateboarding/Biking/Skating - Feels really good, but the negative section below makes this point a little bit moot. 
+ Level design (sans collectibles)

Not so good stuff:

-Difficulty - The game is absurdly easy and you will beat the AI's score by a wide margin every time, which gets boring very quickly.

-Collectibles (incl. graffiti) - To progress in the game, you have to paint graffiti throughout levels. You have to find enough of the predetermined spots to write over to get the attention of that area's crew. Probably a third of my playtime was spent trying to figure out where these damn things are so I could progress to the next boss, rather than actually enjoying the skateboarding/etc aspect of the game. I don't mind if optional collectibles are frustrating to find, but graffiti being the only thing you need to progress kind of sucks.

I really wish progression would've been based on skill instead. Get a certain multiplier, or combo duration, or total score to continue, because the skateboarding/etc aspect of the game is actually very fun but there is no reason to go for high scores unless you're aiming for achievements.

-Police - As you paint graffiti throughout an area, police will arrive and shoot at you. They aren't difficult, but they are very annoying at higher heat levels. You can fight them but the hand-to-hand combat (that exists for some reason) is incredibly boring and slow. If police were removed from the game entirely, it would be an overall improvement.

-Tricks - You can press one of three buttons to do a simple trick. You can combine any of the three with left trigger to do the same trick but get more points. There aren't any interesting combos, there's no real depth, you just press buttons to get points. It's not like points really matter much anyway because you will win every time by just button mashing.

-Health - You are essentially immortal, but you do have a health bar that regens very quickly if you do take damage. Aside from the final boss, the only time I ever actually ran out of health and died was when my character got stuck in place (only happened once, not a recurring bug) and police shot me until I died. This feels like a completely useless mechanic alongside police in general.

Just can't get enuff? Pretty easily, actually, and after that it becomes very obvious how shallow and – as the result – unexciting the game really is. Yes, I played through it but the process began to feel like chore and an annoyance after the initial infatuation wore off.

Got them vibes? Yes, the game's visual design is on point – excellent, really – and a perfect example of how good design and vision can easily trump graphical fidelity. You either enjoy the music or you don't, depending on your personal preferences – though Hideki Naganuma again shines – but in either case, the soundtrack still feels very well curated and fits the game. If the music wears out its welcome for you, though, you immediately realize just how bare-bones the sound design of the game is without any. New Amsterdam is a quiet city – not just in terms of audio but also because it feels that way overall.

Got them moves? Unfortunately... no. BRC borrows a TON from Jet Set Radio (Future) which would be fine if it did things notably better now, 20+ years later – along with doing NEW things – but unfortunately it doesn't. (By comparison, JSR still felt like a lot of fun, even without having any nostalgy for it.) Instead, most of the game's gameplay ideas – borrowed or not – don't seem like they've been considered properly which leaves you with an unsatisfying, lukewarm experience playing an easy, basic collect-a-thon that doesn't engage or challenge you (and I'm writing this as someone who's mediocre at games, at best).

The movement, tricks and combos – if you can call them that – have little nuance, and there's no real sense of challenge or progression at any point of the game. Playing the game is no different at endgame than when you first start; apart from shortcuts, all pick-ups and unlocks are – as far as I could tell – purely cosmetic and the game doesn't really introduce much new along the way. A game doesn't HAVE to do that by any means if its mechanics are sound, but if it doesn't, you shouldn't feel like you're missing something while you play either.

Combat is plain bad and feels glued on; bosses are poorly designed – ranging from annoying to boring to forgettable, or all of the above – and there's literally no point to ever fight cops because they neither pose a threat or a challenge, nor do you really have anything to gain if you do engage them. You'd think being hunted by beat cops, riot cops, snipers and robots all gunning for you would be an exciting challenge but it really isn't, and you're more likely to just try to ignore them. And that's what the game basically encourages you to do – although it likely wasn't intended. The cops showing up culminates in either you dying (which happens rarely if ever, as it's pretty difficult to do) or, typically, you changing your outfit; what a climax. "If you do vandalism, you'll get in annoying trouble. If you then challenge the cops that show up, you'll only get in even more annoying trouble. And most importantly, there is no way for you to actually come out on top with them," the gameplay practically tells you; truly fitting for a game with anti-establishment, cyberpunk themes. It feels like the game primarily has cops because JSR had them without properly considering HOW they actually should function within the game. It's similar to how most of its systems feel – half-baked – which is a shame.

I doubt that BRC would have nearly the (incredibly) positive reviews it does now if people didn't want JSR3 so badly and if the game wasn't riding on JSRF's coattails so hard. It's a real bummer to say this because the game DOES feel like a labor of love and a genuine effort, but it needed to do more than just try to (too superficially) copy JSRF, especially at the hefty price it's being sold.

This is another time where I wish the "Informative" option was available for regular reviews instead of only being there for curators. But I am gonna complain, so I guess this is a negative review.

It just doesn't give me what I bought the game for. I wanted fun combos like Tony Hawk Pro Skater and fun platforming like Jet Set Radio Future. I got neither. The combos hinge entirely on you accumulating boost meter to do the boost moves which are the only way to get points, rather than hinging on how long you can keep a combo going, with as many moves as possible. 

The scoring system was pure bullshit, by the way. It only increases its multiplier if you touch a billboard or you *lean into a curve on a rail*. So not how many *tricks* you can do. Or how varied the chain is. No, your multiplier is entirely driven by doing every single corner in the level to acquire a multiplier because you start spamming boost dash moves to reach the achievement requirement.

The platforming is also not there because they've made the levels humongous and barren, leading to you having to basically manual your way to every rail because the longest unbroken chain of rails in the game you can do is maybe 4 short ones in the first level. The best levels was the Pyramid, and that's only because it's  small enough that there's actually skips and techs you can do in it with loads of ramps to jump around on. There are very few times where you need to manual on that level.

Also why the hell are there so many inward-facing billboard chains? Like that's supposed to be a forbidden tech in the original games but in this one, apparently, dashing backwards into the poster that was facing away from the one you just jumped off is just how the game is actually meant to be. In fact, why were posters so rare in general? There were so many spots that could have been improved by having posters to jump between.

You also have the graffiti system from Jet Set Radio except they forgot the reason why it worked in Jet Set Radio was because it's an extremely slow game where enemies will actually try to stop you from tagging stuff. In this game, you go fast as fuck boosting everywhere to the point where the most dangerous police enemy is the turrets that stop you from just leaving. And when you go fast as fuck, that tagging just breaks the flow. You should have had it be only for L-XL graffitis so you can place those ones that you have to stop for in meaningful spots, instead of having us pause in mid air just to do circles on the joystick.

I don't understand the point of the heat system being in the game. Like it genuinely is just a minor nuisance the entire time. It would have been much more impactful to have properly designed police battles throughout the game instead of randomly deciding "You have to fight police snipers now but one of them is wearing a white helmet actually". And speaking of the police:

Where the hell is the voice acting for cutscenes? I've had Tryce exposition dump me the entire layout and plot of every zone I go to, but he's just not doing the Professor K narration. He just *subtitles* as if he was doing a Professor K voice. This is relevant  to the previous section because the police assaults are just missing the aesthetics of HQ TO ALL SQUADS. Like I don't even notice the police is on me until the turret cutscene plays. You got the heat system from GTA. Did you miss the part where GTA has police radio chatter when the chase starts? Or would that have ruined that little late game joke where the character says he can't listen to police radio chatter?

Also, the police fights are just worthless. Like it is just not fun to run back and forth boost dashing to knock them down. The Golden Rhinos had to be boost dashed because they were late game enemies, I do not want to boost dash a basic police officer 3 times to get them down. Also for the next game you can just remove the attack buttons, no one is doing that, that's garbage. Just make enemies with a clear "stun" condition that lets you tag them. You did it with the robot enemies and they're fun to fight.

They put mumble rap in the soundtrack. I don't think they know why any more than we do. I think they saw rap was on the Jet Set Radio Future soundtrack and wanted to emulate that but they forgot one very important component: Aisle 7 was the song for Rokkaku-dai Heights. It perfectly fit the vibe of skating down in the slums during late afternoon. Rocking the Mic was the song for the sewers. It perfectly fit the vibes of hopping half pipes and random power cables in the sewer system. There is not a level where mumble rap fits. Or rap in general. None of them have *that vibe*. So, soundtrack fails a vibe check on some of the songs. But at least *your* Birthday Cake was not atrocious.

The graffiti markers were very buggy the entire time and I don't know why they got rid of the hovering arrow/circle system that was in the Jet Set Radio games because it made it easy to tell from the side that you have to tag this wall. And also since it's a physical object it's much less prone to shader bugs.

The character designs are questionable. You start the game as *some guy* then you get the robot head which is sick, but then, you turn back into *some guy*. Like imagine the most generic looking hipster you can. The kind that wears a beanie. That is your main character when he doesn't have his robot head on. Now imagine a youtuber that grooms children. That is what the main character looked like before having the robot head. Then you meet *some guy in a winter coat* and *some girl* in a winter coat and you fight *some girls in a winter coat*, because apparently winter coats are just peak design. There's also alot of overdesigning going on. Like Solace has the whole crash test dummy aesthetic and the happy merchant face... And then also angel wings, for some reason. Rave looks really cool, until you turn her around and you see her goofy ass  helmet htat has no reason to be there. Rise straight up wears a bathing suit underneath a winter coat, what is it with these winter coats? Mesh is a random bald kid in an oversized t-shirt wearing a VR headset who screams LESSGOOOOOO and LESKETTIT, which you would be extremely familiar with if you watch twitch, and he's one of the more coherent designs.

Oh, right speaking of Twitch, there's alot of zoomer lingo that does not age well in this game. One of the character says "yaaaas". That hasn't been a thing in like 5 years. Another of the characters also says "fam". *Also* hasn't been a thing in a few years.

Overall, it really just seems like everything they tried to do differently was done differently for the sake of being different, without understanding why it was done that way in the original games they got the ideas from.

Anyways, I recommend it if you're looking for "An indie game in the same genre as Jet Set Radio", but I absolutely cannot recommend it if you're looking for a spiritual successor to jet set radio. The vibes failed, the funk is not present.
